body: Somebody fed the jukebox a quarter before the game sound came up, and the Meters come out of it loose and bright and a hair ahead of the beat, a New Orleans street parade turning the corner into a sports bar on Mission Street at five past ten on a Sunday morning. Then the kickoff comes up on every television in the place and buries it, and the parade goes on underneath for anybody still listening. Lena is still listening. She’s doing the horn part under her breath.

Jack is in yesterday’s clothes. He hasn’t been to bed. He came down Mission on the 11 with clementine still on his fingers, and the table Lena is holding is the one under the brass bell, with the rope already off its cleat and wound once around her fist, because the owner has learned.
She’s in black and gold with the cardigan over it, and her voice is all the way back. She’s spending it on the opening kickoff.

“Youngstown.” It’s exactly how she says it on any Sunday, and after half past four this morning that’s its own kind of weather. She hooks the chair across from hers out from the table with the toe of her boot, and he sits in it.

Laney is beside her in a Pi Lam sweatshirt with last night’s semiformal still on her lashes and a single tan Ugg in her lap like a handbag. She reaches into it and comes out with a clementine. “Don’t,” she tells Jack, peeling it. “Somebody broke into my *shoes*, Jack. I am in *mourning*. This is my brunch of mourning.” She lifts the Ugg off her lap. “This one’s evidence. The other one’s still at the scene.” She looks at him over the peel for longer than anybody looks at an innocent man. Lena is very interested in the first series.

Kevin has the end of the table, the napkin scorebook squared in front of him and a golf pencil beside it, and his Odyssey keys back on his own ring, Bellarmine lanyard and all. He sets them down by the napkin. “Doug’s Croc,” he says. “On a bed of chocolate coins.” He looks at Jack once, a look with a question in it, and keeps the question, and writes SAINTS at the top of one column and WASHINGTON at the top of the other.
“Julian’s leaving Oakland after lunch,” Lena tells the table. “His mama won’t let anybody up while there’s food on it, and there’s always food on it. He’ll text me a cow.”
“A cow,” Jack says.
“Every time he drives the 101. It’s a tradition. There are a lot of cows.”

At the end of the bar Dale Wisniewski is on his stool in the Barry Sanders jersey, and the owner has put the Lions on the set over the dartboard, against the Bengals, at the same hour — a porch light left on for him.

The Saints are at Washington, and for most of the first half Washington plays like a team that hasn’t read the papers. Just before the half Brees throws one straight into a Redskin’s hands, and the bar groans, and then Meachem, who was supposed to catch it, runs the man down from behind and takes it back off him — takes it right out of his arms, like a coat off a hook — and runs it the other way into the end zone.
Lena is up on the rung of her chair before the owner can nod, ringing it with both fists.
“He *stole* it,” Lena says, to the room. “That’s *legal*?”
Kevin, writing it down: “It’s encouraged.”

At the half Laney gives the table the Pi Lam semiformal in three acts. “Sloane’s date wore a *kilt*, y’all. He is not Scottish. He is from Newport Beach. Somebody asked him what was under it and he said *tradition*.” A sophomore cried in the coat check over a boy who wasn’t there. The DJ played “Single Ladies” four times, and the fourth time was personal. Lena laughs at all of it, and Kevin writes HALF in the margin and says, “Four times is a pattern,” and Laney points a clementine section at him across the table. “*Thank* you, Kevin.”

The third quarter belongs to Washington. Laney finishes the clementine and finds a second one in the toe of the Ugg. Along the bottom of the screen the crawl keeps bringing Cleveland around, San Diego ahead of the Browns at home, and Jack reads it every time it comes by. It doesn’t get better. At five past one the Lions game goes final on the set over the dartboard, and Dale says, from his stool, “Bengals. It had to be the Bengals.” Jack lifts his coffee to him down the length of the bar, and Dale lifts his glass back.

Late in the fourth Washington is up seven, with the ball close enough to kick it and put the whole thing away, and their kicker comes out for a field goal so short the bar goes quiet out of something like respect. He misses it. Laney, who has not followed one down of this all day, is on her feet anyway, holding the Ugg over her head. Lena has her eyes shut and both hands around the rope. “*Thank* you, Jesus. Sorry. *Thank* you.”

Brees gets the ball back with the clock running. He throws it long down the sideline, to Meachem again, and Meachem has it in the end zone, and Sully’s comes up out of its chairs. Lena rings with one hand. Her other hand comes off the table, across it, and lands on Kevin’s shoulder, and grips that. The kick ties it.
Kevin prints it on the napkin in capitals: OT — SUDDEN DEATH (SUNDAY, ADVENT II).

Under it, before he puts the golf pencil down, he adds a line in the same capitals: COSTIGAN — PRESENT. Lena reads it upside down and doesn’t take her eyes off the screen for long. “Sit tight,” she says. “You haven’t seen how this one ends.”

In overtime nobody does anything for a while. Then Washington’s fullback catches one in the flat and gets turned upside down, and the ball comes out of him, and the officials go under the hood for so long that Laney finds a third clementine. When they come out from under it it’s the Saints’ ball on Washington’s thirty-seven. A handful of plays later, at twenty-five past one, Hartley jogs out to kick an eighteen-yard field goal, about the distance from their table to the bathrooms. The holder kneels. Lena has the rope in both fists.

body: Low December sun comes through the blind in bars and lies across the bed, and Jack wakes up in it not knowing what day it is. He’s on top of the covers in his clothes, and over him, tucked in at the shoulder, there’s a gray cashmere throw that isn’t his. It lives folded on the end of Theo’s bed. He has never seen it unfolded.
The RAZR is in his right fist, shut. He lay down holding it, somewhere around two, with two texts on it he meant to answer.
Theo is at the MacBook in the navy robe with his back to the room. Over the desk Rosie’s princes are still taped up by all four corners, and against the lamp there’s still a clementine, drying out.
“You were holding it like a rosary,” Theo says.
He scrolls. “Twelve and oh, I’m told. Laney sent it in capitals. And then, separately, a picture of a boot.”
It’s twenty to four. He has lost the afternoon somewhere between the bus and the pillow, and down the hall somebody’s television has the late games on loud enough to follow. Jack opens the phone.

s03.slug: SUNDAY · 6:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL
body: The east-stairwell landing has the only good reception on four, so it’s where the calls home happen: the top step, the cinderblock cold through his shirt, the window open its six inches on the dark over the Lagoon. Ten past six here. Ten past nine on Glenwood Avenue, and his mother has been home from Trumbull since three.
“Your father drove,” she says. “He waited in the truck again.” And straight on: “Did you eat?”
“I ate.”

“Don’t lie to me, I can hear it in your voice.” She lets it go, because there’s news. The officer at the desk asked after Nonna. Nonna is asleep in her chair with the cast on the afghan. Rosie found an orange and a chocolate coin in each of her shoes this morning, ate both coins before Mass, and is keeping the oranges for reasons she won’t give. “Your father did my shoe,” his mother says. “I won two dollars.”
“How’s Danny?”

“He’s good. He says the food’s the same.” Paper moves on the oilcloth. “Hang on. I wrote it down. I wrote it on the back of an envelope in the truck so I’d get it right.” She reads it to him slowly, word for word, as it was given to her. “Your brother says to tell you he went to the library. He says, quote, ‘She raised peacocks and she was mean and I like her.’ Unquote. He says is it still something.” The paper goes down. “And tell the rich one Reggie says hi. What’s still something, Jack?”
“Danny’s being Danny.”

He can see it, though: his brother at a bolted table in the prison library with a paperback somebody else has already underlined, looking up a dead woman from Georgia because Jack said her name across a visiting room.

On the line there’s the click he knows, the upstairs extension coming up off its cradle in the hands of somebody who believes she’s being careful, and then a sound like a cough with a scream folded up inside it.
“Regina, hang up the phone.”
“I’m *not on the phone*.”
From the front room, sharp, Nonna’s voice carries the length of the house. “*E l’attrice?*”
“Ma, go to bed.” His mother, away from the phone, and then back to it: “She means the girl on Gina’s show. She thinks they’re real people.”
The extension makes its noise again.
Out on the Lagoon path a bike light goes along the far shore, and Jack follows it till the trees take it.
“The phone bill came Saturday,” his mother says.

He can hear the pen. She has it flat on the kitchen table with the lamp pulled down over it, going down it line by line with a tick beside each one. She does the collection ledger at St. Brigid’s the same way, Mondays.
“Four hundred and nine text messages, Jack.”
“Ma —”
“It’s pages. You have your own section. Your sister has a section and a half, and she’s fifteen, and I understand your sister.” Up on the extension, very carefully, nobody breathes.
“Your father isn’t mad. Your father’s *curious*.”
From the other room, over the television: “I’m not curious.”
“He’s curious. He’s watching the highlights so he can lose twice.” The pen stops. “Who is it?”

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something.

choices.key: Your mother counted four hundred and nine texts on the November bill and asked who. You told her: a girl.
response: “A girl, Ma.”
“Is it Lena?”
“No.”
A silence on Glenwood Avenue, long enough that he hears the furnace come on under the kitchen floor.
“…Okay,” his mother says. “Is she nice?”
“No.”
“*Jack.*”
“She’s not *nice*, Ma. She’s —” Out the window the far shore of the Lagoon has two lights on it. “Something.”
His mother breathes out, close to the phone. “That’s what your father said about me.”
She doesn’t ask a name. The pen goes on the envelope, a short line of it, and stops.
Before she lets him go she says, “Lena’s saint is in Nonna’s missal now. The one in red. She keeps her place with it.”
And from the recliner in the other room, over the television, his father: “One and eleven.”
After they hang up he stays on the top step with the RAZR shut in his hand and the window letting the cold in on him. He knows without the itemized pages whose most of them were.

s04.slug: SUNDAY · 9:55 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE COURTYARD
body: At the nine o’clock the Gospel is Luke, the voice crying in the desert — *every valley shall be filled* — and Kenzie Rourke takes the psalm on her guitar with the capo so far up the neck it sounds like a mandolin with a head cold. Joey Abruzzo gets the second violet candle lit on his third match, and the front pew sits back. Two rows behind Lena, beside Kevin, Jack watches Julian Park-Ellis — down from Oakland since the afternoon, and still in the sweater he drove five hours in — answer every response by ear, half a breath behind the room, and land on every one.

By ten the cold has settled into the courtyard for the night. The olive tree, the low wall under it, the sprinkler head standing up dead out of a crust of dried mud: somebody shut it off at the valve back in November. Kevin peels off at the door — “Orgo,” he says, with real regret — and goes up Ocean Road at a jog with his hands in his quarter-zip.

Lena is on the wall in her coat with her boots crossed at the ankle, the black mantilla folded small in one fist, and the little green Loeb on her knee, shut on its pencil. Two days to Book Nine, on what can’t have been more than three hours’ sleep. She looks up when Jack comes out, and back down at the Loeb.

Julian comes out through the propped door with two coffees in Newman mugs, the white ones with the little leather boat on the side. He sets one in Lena’s hands. He sees Jack, and holds the other one out to him without a word about it, and goes back in for a third.
Jack stands with the mug warming his palms. The coffee is Mrs. Fitch’s. It has been on since the five o’clock, and it tastes like it went to both Masses.

When Julian comes back he sits on the wall beside Lena, not close, and blows on his cup. “I heard the end of it in Gilroy,” he tells Jack. “On the radio, at a Chevron by the freeway. A man from Washington missed a kick, and the man on the radio said a word you can’t say at a church.”
“He didn’t miss it,” Lena says. “God reached down out of the sky over Maryland and moved that ball four inches. I watched Him do it. Kevin watched Him do it.”
“She texted me the number,” Julian says. “Just the number. In capitals.”
“Twelve is a holy number,” Lena says. “Twelve tribes. Twelve apostles.”
“One of the apostles was Judas,” Jack says.

“And they replaced him. By lot. And the lot fell on Matthias, and nobody’s heard a word about Matthias since, which is exactly what you want in a kicker.” She drinks her coffee, satisfied, and bumps Julian’s knee with hers. “Tell him about Daniel.”

“He’s good.” Julian turns the mug by the boat. “He got in Thursday. My mother’s cooked for a battalion. He brought her a flag that flew on his ship, folded in a triangle, and she didn’t know where to put it, so it’s on the piano. Nothing’s ever been allowed on the piano.” He turns the mug the other way. “He says the Navy’s mostly waiting.” A small smile at the coffee. “I told him so is music.”
“Tell him about the cow,” Lena says.
“I saw the cow,” Jack says. “Upside down. At Sully’s.”
“It was a good cow,” Julian says, mildly, as if somebody had suggested otherwise. “It was standing by itself in a field behind the Chevron, looking at the freeway. I thought she’d want to know.”

Then he looks up at Jack, with the calm that makes people trust him with their cars and their dogs and their bad news. “Thursday,” he says. “Bastille. I finished it.” A look down at the cup. “The new one.”
He doesn’t look at Lena when he says it. Lena is looking at the olive tree.
“Will you stay to the end?”
In Jack’s coat pocket the RAZR has *tomorrow. im asking* in it, and Thursday is four days off, and the coffee is going cold in his hands.

“Good,” says Julian. Lena drinks her coffee.

They break up at the gate onto Ocean Road. Julian takes the three mugs back in, hooked on his fingers by their handles, and Lena waits for him at the gate with the Loeb under her arm, and Jack is the one who goes. Behind him, before he’s off the curb: “Twelve and oh, Youngstown.”
He turns around in the empty road and walks the next two steps backward. “Twelve and oh.”

body: The storm gets there before he’s awake. It comes in sideways off the Lagoon and throws itself at the window by the bucketful, and the glass shudders in its frame, and he lies under it working out what the noise is: rain, real rain, the first of the winter, the kind Youngstown would call a Monday. Down on Anacapa Way the gutters have already given up, and somebody’s bike is lying on its side in the lot where the wind put it.
“Take the umbrella,” says the shape under Theo’s duvet. “Top shelf. It’s Burberry; it has a personality.”

The top shelf of Theo’s closet is the gray camera bag, a shoebox with COOKIES — DON’T behind it, a black duffel, and along the front edge an umbrella with its crook hanging over. Jack hooks it down, and the crook brings the strap of the black duffel with it, and the bag tips out over the lip of the shelf and hangs there, its zipper open two inches on denim, and on the collar of the denim a small enamel pin, a red Ferris wheel and FRESNO FAIR.
He pushes the bag back square on the shelf.
“The *umbrella*, Costigan.”
“Got it.”
“With all its spokes,” the duvet says. “It’s been to Ascot.”

He takes the navy blazer down off its hanger, the Goodwill one from Market Street that does for Mass and for Hale, and puts it over his arm under the umbrella, and goes out to the east landing. The window there is shut against the weather, with a laminated card taped to the sill in Priya’s font — WINDOW TO REMAIN CLOSED DURING RAIN EVENTS — and the rain has come in under it anyway and lies in a bright line along the sill. Outside, it’s coming down the glass in ropes, and the RAZR finds its bar and gives him what came in before eight.

s06.slug: MONDAY · 2:35 PM · THE SAAB, OCEAN ROAD → THE 101 SOUTH
body: The rain is coming in off the Channel in gray sheets, one behind another, walking up over the bluff and flattening the ice plant on their way inland, and at the Marine Lab turnout the chain across the service drive is streaming. The Saab is nosed up to it with the top up. Up, the top is mostly tape: silver along one seam, black along the next, and over the passenger side a strip of blue painter’s tape where somebody ran out of both.

He gets in with the umbrella fighting him to the last rib, and the blazer folded over his arm, dry except for one cuff. Skye is behind the wheel in a man’s raincoat with the sleeves turned back four times, over something pink and quilted that he looks at once — “Don’t,” she says — and her hair is wound up on her head with a Sharpie stuck through the knot. A paperback *Little Women* is on his seat with a gas receipt in it about a third of the way through. She moves it to the dash as he sits.
“Beth’s still alive,” she says. “I’m reading slow.”
She looks up at the canvas over their heads. It shudders every time the wind gets under a seam. “The rule is top down,” she says. “The rule has met the rain.”

At the light by the on-ramp the roof finds his left knee. One cold drop through the seam over his head, then another in the same place, then another, steady as a kitchen faucet with a bad washer, into the denim. The defroster is blowing at the windshield as hard as it can and losing; she wipes a porthole in the fog with the raincoat’s cuff and drives through that.

South of town the 101 goes down through Gaviota Pass between walls of black rock with water coming off them in ropes, and comes out along the Channel, and the afternoon goes gray in layers: the road, the water beside the road, the place where the islands ought to be. Trucks throw up spray that hangs behind them like smoke. She drives fast anyway, in the left lane, both hands on the wheel.

“It’s a camera test,” she says, when he asks. “Not an audition. I already got through the audition. Now they need to know if the camera likes me in a dress from 1962 when I’m sad.” She passes a horse trailer with a horse’s rear end in it, blanketed against the wet. “The camera has always liked me sad. It’s a whole problem.”
“Which scene?”
“The last one. The rain.”
“She forgives him.”

“In forty buttons.” She takes a hand off the wheel and draws a line from her throat down to her lap. “Here’s your character. You’re my cousin from Ohio. You’ve come out to see the industry. You’re very shy and you wash dishes.”
“I do wash dishes.”
“That’s what makes it work.” She makes a small, exact shape in the air with her fingers. “*Specificity.*”

Past Refugio the white iPhone lights up in the cup holder and says MOM. She lets it ring once and most of a second time. Her thumb goes to the speaker and stops there, and she picks the phone up instead and wedges it between her ear and her shoulder and puts both hands back on the wheel.
“Hi, Mom.”
Her voice has gone up for it: brighter, quicker, half a step up, a girl answering the phone in somebody’s kitchen with her homework done.

“Driving. No, I’m being careful. I’m in the slow lane.” She is in the fast lane. “Wednesday’s fine. What time? I’ll be there. I’ll eat first.” She listens. A green sign goes over them, unreadable in the rain. “The reunion picture? Everybody? Sure. Sure, Mom, that’s fine.” She listens longer. The wipers go.

None of the bright goes out of it. “She changed it *back*?” Jack looks out at the Channel. “No. No, it’s fine. *New Moon* is fine.” She laughs, a pleasant laugh that would go over well on any phone. “I know she does. Tell her thanks.” A truck passes on the right and throws a sheet of water over the glass, and she drives blind through it without a flicker. “Love you, Mom.”

She drops the phone back in the cup holder with the screen to the seat, and drives a mile. On the curve past El Capitan *Little Women* slides across the dash toward him, and she reaches out and puts it back where it was, and keeps her hand on it till the road straightens.

A Ralphs truck comes up on the right, throwing spray, and she lifts her chin at it. “Gil,” she says. “Married to a woman who picks out his shirts. He hasn’t chosen a shirt since 1979, and if you asked him what color he likes, he’d have to call home.”

At Carpinteria the flags over a car lot hang at half-staff for Pearl Harbor, too wet to stir. At the Rincon the road runs along a shelf of boulders with the ocean right up against it, and today the ocean is coming over. The surf throws itself up the riprap gray and white and slides back off across the shoulder in sheets, and she moves them over a lane. Ventura goes by low and wet. Past it, where the road leaves the water and starts across the flat green fields toward the hills, she finds a station that comes in, and turns it up.

It’s a woman singing high and quick over a guitar, about being a long way off somewhere and wanting not to be, and Skye knows every word. Jack doesn’t know it at all. When it comes around to *coming home* she sings it at the windshield, under the woman, low, with her eyes on the road, and her face is nothing like it was on the phone.

On the Conejo Grade the wind comes across the hills broadside and leans on the car, and the canvas over his head snaps and fills, and the blue tape over the seam lifts at one corner. The drip on his knee is a thin, steady stream now. She sees it. She keeps climbing.

body: Burbank in the rain at twenty to six is every gutter on the block running at once. The block is warehouses: a prop house with a fiberglass horse in its fenced yard under a blue tarp, a lumber yard with its gate chained, and in the middle a long beige building with no windows and a 9 painted on its side three stories tall.
A guard sits at the gate in a plywood shed with a space heater going at his shins. He slides his window back and looks at her and nowhere else. “Evening, Miss Callender. Some night.”
“My cousin from Ohio,” Skye says.

Only then does the guard look past her, at Jack in the passenger seat with one wet knee. He runs his pen down a list on his clipboard to a line — CALLENDER, S. + 1 — and holds out a paper visitor pass with a clip on it. She takes it, pulls the Sharpie out of her hair, writes on the pass in capitals against the steering wheel, pushes the Sharpie back into the knot, and hands it to Jack. MY COUSIN FROM OHIO.
“Where people can see it,” she says.
Over the stage door there’s a red bulb in a wire cage, dark. “When that’s on, you don’t open the door. You don’t sneeze. You don’t be from anywhere.”

Inside, the storm is louder. It’s on the roof, three stories up, a hard steady roar over the dark of the grid, and under the grid, under a hundred lamps hung off pipes, somebody has built 1962. A canvas revival tent stands in the middle of the stage with one side rolled up: a sawdust aisle between rows of folding chairs, a piano with the ivory gone off two keys, a plywood pulpit, and over it a banner in house paint, JESUS SAVES — ALL WELCOME. Through the tent’s far flap a parking lot is painted on the floor with three cars from the year on it — a Ford, a Studebaker with its chrome taped over so it won’t flare, a pickup with a dog crate in the bed — and over the cars, on a crane arm, a rain tower: a row of pipes with sprinkler heads in it, dripping from the last test into a plastic kiddie pool somebody has set under the worst of it. It is going to rain in here tonight, under a roof that’s being rained on. Jack seems to be the only one who thinks that’s funny.

Wardrobe takes her. When she comes back she’s in a cape at a mirror beside the tent with a woman setting her hair into 1962, pins in the woman’s mouth, and from then on the stage wants things from her, one after another, and Jack stands behind the mirror and watches them come.

The hair woman takes the pins out of her mouth and holds out a flip phone with stickers on it. “My niece’s. She’s twelve. She made me bring it. Would you —” “Say it like Cassidy?” Skye takes the phone and thumbs through to the greeting, and out of her comes somebody else entirely, sweet and a half-step high, a girl from a lake who hopes you’re having a nice day. *Hi! You’ve reached Brianna! She can’t come to the phone, but she’s so glad you called.* It’s perfect. The hair woman puts a hand over her heart.

A producer’s assistant, with a magazine — her face on the cover from some summer, a bikini top and a great deal of lip gloss — and a silver pen. *To Kayla’s mom.* An agent’s assistant, holding out a phone: a car service will be at the gate at one to take her home. “I drove.” “They’re sending it anyway.” “Then it can follow me.” A grip with a sandbag on his shoulder whose nephew has written a script, a really good one, about a dog that solves crimes. She writes the nephew’s email on the back of her hand.

And all through it people raise their phones. A BlackBerry, a Motorola, somebody’s iPhone held sideways. Every time one comes up her face goes to the same place for it — chin down, eyes up, the smile — and holds there for the click, and comes back.

Jack finds the coffee, a long table against the wall with a man in an apron guarding the shrimp, and the man in the apron looks at his blazer and asks if he’s network. “Cousin,” Jack says. The man reads his lapel. “Ohio,” he says, with real sympathy, and lets him have a shrimp. Jack brings her a coffee, black, and puts it in her hand under the cape. When a PA gives her two stapled pages to look at while her hair sets, she can’t hold them and the coffee both, so he holds the pages up at her eye level and turns to the second one when she nods. “My sides,” she says. “You’re holding my sides.” Once a PA going by hands him a coil of cable and points, and he carries it where the PA pointed and comes back, and in the mirror she watches him go and come back with her coffee stopped halfway to her mouth. When the last phone goes down she finds him in the mirror, behind her with page two, and her face is the one from the car.

The director comes through in a scarf, indoors, and frames the tent with his fingers, and frames her, and once, passing, frames Jack. The boy who plays the thief looks about twenty-two, with a face Jack is fairly sure he has seen on the side of a bus. He shakes Jack’s hand and calls him cuz. He calls him cuz again on his way past with a plate of shrimp, and seems prepared to keep it up all night.

At ten past seven the first AD, a small woman with a radio on each hip, comes into video village with a problem. The boy’s stand-in is on the 405, and the 405 is a parking lot, and the cinematographer needs a body about six feet tall on the thief’s mark under the rain, now, so he can light Miss Callender’s face against it before they lose the hour. She says this into one of her radios. She is looking at Jack while she says it. So is the cinematographer. So, from the hair chair with pins in her head, is Skye.

It comes out of the pipes colder than the real thing on the roof, and in about four seconds he is wet to the skin in the Goodwill blazer, water running off his nose, while a crew with ladders and light meters lights the girl across from him. She’s on her mark under an umbrella a PA holds over her, in the raincoat over the dress, and for nine minutes by the clock on the slate she doesn’t take her eyes off him. When they cut the water she’s the first one there with a towel.

Between setups Skye finds Jack in the glow of the monitors and mouths it at him across the stage: *union*.

response: He stays behind the monitor. A grip stands in, arms folded, and gets rained on. Every time the bell rings for a new setup she looks for Jack there first, and every time he’s there.

body: The honeywagon is a long white trailer parked against the side of the stage, chopped into rooms the width of a closet, and hers has SKYE on the door on a strip of tape. Inside there’s a mirror ringed in bulbs, a vinyl bench, a counter of pins and powder, and a window the size of a paperback with the rain sheeting down it. The rain on the trailer roof is closer than the rain on the stage, and louder, like sitting inside a drum.

She’s in the dress. White cotton, sleeves to the wrist, a collar that stands up under her jaw, and down the front of it, from the hem to the throat, forty buttons covered in the same white cotton, every one of them done.
“Forty,” she says. “Hem to chin. They didn’t want anybody getting to her before the end of the second act.” She shuts the door with her heel.
She backs him onto the squeaking bench and comes down after him with a knee on either side of him on the vinyl and the skirt going everywhere, yards of it, over his legs and the bench and the floor.

body.text: He’s still wet. The blazer is soaked through and his shirt is stuck to him under it, and she takes a lapel in each fist and wrings them out, hard, onto the floor of the trailer. “I watched you stand in that for nine minutes,” she says. “I’ve been waiting an hour to do that.”

body: Her lipstick is somebody’s idea of 1962, a dark rose, and it’s on him almost at once, and she lets it be. When his hand goes to her collar she catches it. “No buttons,” she says against his mouth. “Wardrobe counted them. They’ll *know*.”

So his hands go everywhere the buttons aren’t. The small of her back, warm through the cotton. Her wrists, where the sleeves end and her pulse is going under his thumbs. Her jaw, and the soft place under it where the collar stops and his mouth can get to. The backs of her knees under the hem, bare, where she makes a sound into his neck that isn’t in anybody’s script.

She keeps score. Every time his hand strays toward the front of the dress she calls the button by its number — “Nine. Careful. *Twenty-two*” — and the numbers get worse on purpose, until by her count the dress has sixty-one buttons and he has been near every one of them. She’s laughing against his mouth; she stops laughing. She kisses him slower, and harder, with both hands in his hair and her weight coming down on him through all that cotton, and he holds her by the backs of the knees and forgets what number they were on. He wants her badly enough to say so and hasn’t got the breath to.

Somebody knocks on the trailer door, three times, polite. Through the little window the somebody is a yellow rain slicker under an umbrella, waiting on the metal step. “Skye? They’re ready for you in the rain.”

“Coming,” she says, in an entirely reasonable voice, with one hand still in his hair. Then she’s up and at the mirror, fixing a collar that was never crooked, running a finger down the front of the dress and counting under her breath, and getting forty. She does her mouth in one stroke. She looks at his in the mirror. “Makeup’s going to have questions.”
She has her hand on the latch.

choices.text: Catch her wrist at the door.
response: He catches her wrist, and she turns around into it, and it’s once more, hard, against the trailer door, with the PA standing on the other side of it on the metal step. “*Cousin*,” she says into his mouth, and goes.

choices.text: “I’d like to stay in here all night.”
response: She stops with her hand on the latch and looks back at him on the bench, under the bulbs, with her lipstick on him. “People in this trailer say *how long have we got*,” she says, and goes out into the rain to forgive somebody.

choices.text: Let her go. Sit there till your heart slows.
response: She goes. He sits on the vinyl in the ring of bulbs with the rain on the roof. In the mirror there’s a man in a Goodwill blazer with a girl’s 1962 lipstick on his mouth, and Jack looks at him until his heart slows.

s07b.slug: MONDAY · 10:30 PM · STAGE 9, THE TENT IN THE RAIN
body: Take four. The rain comes out of the pipes in a white curtain under the lamps, loud on the painted asphalt, and through it the preacher’s daughter comes out of the tent and finds the boy who stole from the plate, standing by the Studebaker with the money in his fist. She says his name. He turns around. She forgives him, and she cries.

She’s good. Nothing extra and everything where it goes, like his father under a hood. The tears come when she wants them, on the word she wants them on, and run down the same cheek the same way, take after take. Take five, the same. The made rain makes its own weather: a cold mist drifts off it as far as video village and settles on the monitors, and between takes a PA goes down the row wiping the screens with a chamois, so that every time Jack watches her cry he watches it through somebody’s wiping. After each one the director comes out of his chair and goes to her in the rain with his palms pressed together, and when the water shuts off Jack can hear what he says, because it’s the same every time. *More grace. Give me more grace.* Jack has been asking for the same thing since the second grade. He never thought to try it in a scarf.

body.text: Jack watches from video village in a borrowed crew jacket three sizes wrong, his blazer hung on a light stand behind him, dripping onto the cables.

body: Before take five the boy who plays the thief comes to video village with water running out of his hair and leans in at Jack’s elbow. “Cuz. Is she always this good?” “As long as I’ve known her,” Jack says, which is true, and the boy nods, satisfied, at the family history. While they reset the rain they bring her to the monitors in a towel. She stands at Jack’s shoulder behind the director’s chair with her hair dripping on the white cotton and watches herself cry on the playback, and when it’s done she says, low, for him only: “What. You’re making a face.”

choices.text: “Nobody forgives anybody in the rain. You forgive somebody the next morning, when it’s dry and nobody’s watching and it costs something.”
response: She stops toweling. She looks at him out of the towel while the rain comes back on behind her. The bell goes for take six, and she walks out into it.

choices.text: “She’s crying because she’s sad. She should be tired. Forgiving somebody is mostly being tired of it.”
response: She hears it out with the towel at her ear. She nods once, slowly, as she did at her pages in the hair chair, and drops the towel over his arm, and the bell goes for take six.
“Liar,” she says, and hands him the towel. The bell goes for take six.

body: Take six: the bell, the red light outside, the rain coming down out of the pipes. On the monitor she comes out of the tent and finds the boy by the Studebaker the same as five times before, and she doesn’t cry.

She’s tired. She looks at the boy across the rain like she has been up all night with what he did and has come out the far side of it, and she reaches up and does the top button of his collar against the wet, one button, with her fingers stiff from the cold. She says the line flat and kind. “It’s all right, Lonnie. Go on home and get dry.” Like it’s the next morning. Like it costs something to say, and she’s paying it.

body.text: Jack hears his own sentence come back to him with her face on it.
body.else: It’s the face he made at the monitor. He’d swear she’s playing that.

body: The stage goes quiet the way St. Brendan’s goes at the consecration, the crew holding still at once, ladders and all, and there’s only the rain on the roof until the director says “Cut,” so softly it barely counts.
The director is out of his chair. “What was *that*?”
Skye has her face in a towel. “My cousin,” she says, into it.
The director turns around in his scarf and finds Jack behind the monitors. “You act?”
“I wash dishes.”
Behind him the boy who plays the thief, dripping, points at Jack and says, “Cuz,” like it settles something.
At two minutes past eleven, in the dark at the back of video village, the phone goes against his leg.

body.text: Book Nine is 566 lines and I know all of them. Pray for me at 8. —L.

body: He reads it with the screen turned in against his chest, where the light can’t go anywhere.

They wrap at twenty to one. The real rain has stopped, and somebody has shut off the other one. Under the rain tower, dead now and dripping into its kiddie pool, she stands in the man’s raincoat with a garment bag over her shoulder and the Sharpie back in her hair.
“So,” she says. “That’s my world.”
“That was a Monday.”

At the gate the guard slides his window back. “Night, Miss Callender. Night, cousin.” Jack wishes him a good night in the voice of a shy man who washes dishes, and she laughs about it till the freeway.

The 101 north is empty and black and shining. Ventura goes by wet, every light in it doubled on the road. She drives with both hands and doesn’t sing. He doesn’t sleep, though twice she tells him he’s allowed.

Past Ventura she catches him looking at the clock on the dash. “What.” “It’s a holy day,” he says. “Since midnight. The Immaculate Conception.” “Is that one of the ones you have to go to?” “That’s one of the ones.” She pulls the Sharpie out of her hair and holds it out to him with her eyes on the road, and then her right hand, palm down, off the wheel. “Write it on me. I want to look it up.” He writes it across the back of her hand in capitals, under the grip’s nephew’s email, with the Saab doing seventy-five, and at the next stretch of streetlights she looks at it and says it over to herself, getting all the syllables in.

body: He types it low against the door while she keeps her eyes on the road. At twenty to four she stops short of the chain at the Marine Lab turnout and lets him out into the dripping ice plant with the engine running and the pass still clipped to his lapel.

body: The fourth floor at four in the morning is a long hum of nothing much: the EXIT sign, the vending machine in the lounge clicking its compressor on, somebody’s alarm clock going off behind a shut door, unanswered. Doug Pruitt is standing under the EXIT sign.

He’s barefoot on the carpet in the Tauren-druid hoodie, with his pillow under one arm, and his eyes are open and there’s no one home in them. His right hand is on the red handle of the pull station, closing.
Jack gets his wrist.
It’s warm and slack and doesn’t fight him. Doug turns his head and smiles at a spot just past Jack’s ear, pleasantly, from very far away.
“Dude,” Doug says. “The raid boss is in the *elevator*.”
“Yeah, Doug,” Jack says. “I’ll tell him.”
“Tell him I brought flasks,” Doug says, with dignity. “He’ll know.”

He takes Doug’s fingers off the handle one at a time. Five alarms since August. Eighteen days, twenty-five, twenty-six, twenty-seven: Margot built an entire science on the spaces in between, with a log and a theory and a stakeout and Gold Bond on the lounge handle and Theo’s camera, and tonight the space is three days, and the science is Doug Pruitt with his pillow, asleep on his feet. Doug yawns without shutting his eyes, which Jack didn’t know a person could do.

His own body has been up since ten to eight on Monday morning, on the tail of a week of short nights, and would like that noted. It ought to be told to somebody. Jack tries it in his head the way it will have to go, on the lawn, under Priya’s headlamp. *I caught him.* At four in the morning? *I was in the hall.* Why were you in the hall? *I was coming in.* From where? *Burbank.* In a blazer? *I was somebody’s cousin.*

The only witness to the end of the semester’s great mystery is standing on the fourth floor at two minutes to four with a Burbank visitor pass in his pocket, holding the culprit by the wrist, and there isn’t a person in this building he can tell how he got here.

journal.title: Doug Pruitt
journal.text: Doug Pruitt. 420, with Kevin. Bakersfield. Mechanical engineering. A Tauren druid. Says ‘dude’ with five vowels. Tuesday the 8th, 3:58 in the morning, I caught his wrist on the east-stair pull station. He was asleep. The raid boss was in the elevator.

Doug lies down on top of his covers with the pillow in both arms, and across the room Kevin breathes on and doesn’t wake.
Down a flight. Jack hasn’t lifted his hand to 305 when it opens. Margot is in black, with a finger in a library book, wide awake and surprised by nothing.
He tells her.
“How do you know?”
“I saw him.”
“At?”
“Four.”
“And at ten to four you came up the front walk in a blazer.” She looks at the blazer. “I assumed a funeral.”
“Go to bed, Costigan. I have a whiteboard to update.”
At a quarter past four he gets into his own bed in the blazer. Across the room Theo is breathing slow and even, and the gray throw is folded on the foot of Theo’s bed where Jack left it.

body: On a holy day the twelve-ten fills like a Sunday that forgot to dress. Noon comes down through the blue glass onto more people than the weekday pews were built for: graduate students on their lunch hour, two nurses in scrubs with their badges turned around, a man in a FedEx uniform on one knee at the end of a pew, freshmen standing three deep along the back wall under the hull. The altar is in white and so is Father Osei, and somebody has put white roses and a gold ribbon at the foot of the Marian shrine in the side aisle. The organist takes the entrance hymn at the speed of a man bringing a boat in against the tide, and the whole church comes in on the *Ave* like a crew.

Mrs. Fitch has her end of the back pew and her purse on her knees, and is giving the standing room a look that says it might have come in October too. Kevin is in the fourth pew on the right, where he always is, with a Bible at the end of it holding the place. He moves it when Jack genuflects.
“Seat,” Kevin whispers.
He keeps his eyes front. “You never answered the Bible,” he whispers, and opens the missalette to the readings.

The first reading is the garden, after the apple: God calling to the man, *Where are you?*, and the man answering that he heard Him, and was afraid, and hid. Then the Gloria, which comes back for a solemnity even in Advent, and which the organist plays as if he’s been saving it since Thanksgiving. Then Luke, and the angel coming in to a girl in a town in Galilee: *Hail, full of grace! The Lord is with you.*

Father Osei comes down out of the ambo for the homily, which he does when he’s serious, and stands in the aisle at the head of the pews with the bad leg taking a rest. “Luke wrote in Greek,” he says, “and I am going to spend three minutes on one Greek word. Then I will let you go back to your examinations, which is a penance I could not improve on.”

“The angel comes into the house and says, *Chaire, kecharitōmenē.* We say, *Hail, full of grace.* Good. But the word is a perfect participle, and a perfect participle is a thing that was done to you, all the way, in the past, and is still true of you now. *Already, and completely, graced.* He does not say, *you will be, if.* He says it is done. And he says it where her name should go.”
He goes over the tense once more, slowly, for the engineers. Then:
“He says it before she has said yes to anything. Before she has done one thing worth putting in a homily. That is the scandal of this feast. God gives first.”

“In Kumasi a physician catches whatever arrives, and I have held a good many newborn children. Not one of them had accomplished anything. Every one of them was loved entirely before it had done a single useful thing, and nearly all of them complained about it at the top of their lungs.” The church laughs, the standing room loudest. “You cannot earn a gift. You can open it.” He looks out at the three deep along the back wall. “Open it.”

At the sign of peace Joey Abruzzo reaches across two pews to pump his hand. “JACK. Holy *day*,” Joey says, at a volume that turns Mrs. Fitch’s head from the back, and goes back to his own pew radiant.
After Communion Jack kneels with his face in his hands and gives Him the list, short, the way it comes: Nonna’s arm. Tariq. Danny. Doug Pruitt’s sleep, whatever Doug Pruitt’s sleep needs.

At the door Osei is shaking hands in his white vestments with the line going out past him into the cold sun. He takes Jack’s hand and keeps it a moment in the doctor’s grip. “Mr. Costigan. On a Tuesday.”
“It’s a holy day, Father.”
“I know,” says Osei. “I was there.”

On the steps Kevin shrugs into his backpack. “Lena’s going tonight,” he says. “The five-thirty, with Julian. She told me after her final.” He points two steps down. “Also, you’re being hunted,” and he’s off toward the library.

Becca is at the bottom of the steps with the clipboard on her hip, and for the length of a sentence she’s shy with him. “Hi. You look like you slept, for once.” After that she’s all clipboard. “You’re on my list.”

They’re everywhere tonight: on the altar, banked in red cups at the Marian shrine, set along the sills of the black windows, and the ribs of the hull overhead catch the light and hold it like the inside of a lantern. The pews are full of people who came straight from the library with their backpacks still on, and the back wall is standing room. The organist is in a tie. Mrs. Fitch is at the door with a stack of worship aids, and hands Jack one off the top. “Not at the twelve-ten, Mr. Costigan,” she says. She was at the twelve-ten. She is at all of them.

Jack gets the end of a pew on the left, behind a family with a baby asleep in a car seat in the aisle. Two pews ahead of him, on the other side of the aisle, is the black lace mantilla. Julian is beside her in a gray cardigan, and when they stand he holds the hymnal open for both of them, low, where she can see it without asking. When they came in he stopped at the end of the pew with one hand on it while she genuflected. He doesn’t genuflect himself. He waits for her to, every time, and goes in after. He has the responses now, all of them, and says them a hair early, proud of them.
The first reading is the garden after the apple — *Where are you?* — and the man who heard, and was afraid, and hid. The Gospel is the angel and the girl. *Hail, full of grace.*

Father Osei preaches from the aisle in his evening voice, which is his noon voice with the lights down. He looks the church over first. “I see some faces from the seven o’clock,” he says, “who are very holy, and a great many faces who were asleep at noon, who are very honest.” The honest ones laugh.

The angel’s word is a perfect participle, he says — *kecharitōmenē*, already and completely graced, before she had said yes to anything, before she had done one thing worth a homily. “Some of you sat examinations today,” he says. “You are waiting to be graded. This is the one feast in the year where the Church tells you the grade came first.” A ripple goes along the backpacks. “Do not think she did not need a Savior. She needed Him first. The rest of us He pulls out of the ditch after we have fallen in. Her He caught on the edge, before she fell. It is the same pair of hands. God gives first. Everything else in her life is what she did with a gift she had already opened. Go and do likewise. Then go and sleep.”
At the sign of peace she turns to the pew behind her and sees Jack over it, two rows back. *Peace be with you*, she mouths, and Julian, turning with her, lifts a hand to Jack across the pews.

At Communion Julian stays in the pew and turns his knees to let her out, and she goes up alone and kneels on the hard floor at the front to receive, the lace forward over her face, and comes back with her hands folded. He moves his knees for her again.

The closing hymn is the one every Catholic in America can sing in their sleep. The organist gives it the full foghorn and the church comes in under him: *Immaculate Mary, your praises we sing.* Julian doesn’t know it. He reads the first verse off the page half a bar behind everybody and comes in on the *Ave* late, and wrong. The second time round he has it — *Ave, Ave* — by ear, off no page, right on it, the easy baritone Jack has heard at Bastille under her alto.
Lena doesn’t turn her head. The lace moves a little at her temple, and she sings the next one louder.

body: The Anchor on a Tuesday night smells of fryer oil on its third day, the Hobart’s steam, and the pot of coffee Gloria puts on at eight for the ones who mean to stay till close. There are six of them tonight, spaced down the counter in their jackets. Gloria isn’t pouring for any of them. She has the register drawer open and a box of paper sleeves from the bank, and she’s rolling nickels on the counter beside the pie case, forty to a sleeve, her lips moving with the count, and she doesn’t stop counting to tell him.
“Thursday you’re off.” A sleeve fills; she crimps the ends shut with her thumbs. “Hector’s girl is due at Christmas, and he wants the hours.”
Jack gets as far as opening his mouth about the plane ticket home.
“Don’t argue with a baby,” Gloria says, and tips out the next forty.
So Thursday is Bastille. He’s already been asked.

He does three hours on the Hobart with the RAZR in the apron. The racks come out of the machine in their own weather, and Rudy’s radio does a ranchera and a used-car commercial and another ranchera, and the six at the counter turn into four and then into a man who eats his pie point-last and takes half an hour about it. Twice Jack dries a hand on his jeans and lays it over the pocket, and takes it off again.

At twenty past nine Rudy wants romaine, and the walk-in is the only door in the Anchor that shuts all the way. Everything else in the place swings: the kitchen doors on their springs, the restroom, the screen onto the back step. The walk-in closes on a steel latch with the sound of a car door, and inside it’s thirty-eight degrees, with a fan grinding away in the ceiling unit, crates of romaine stacked to his shoulder, a case of eggs, Rudy’s flan in a hotel pan under plastic wrap with tomorrow’s date on a strip of masking tape, and his own breath going up white under the caged bulb.

A bathroom he has never been in: a long mirror on the back of a door, a shower curtain with fish on it, yellow and blue, the kind somebody’s mother picks out. Studio City, he’d bet. And her in the mirror, in the white dress from Monday. He knows the collar, and the sleeves to the wrist. Wardrobe counted forty buttons out to her, and she has undone all forty, throat to hem, and there’s nothing under the dress but a strip of white cotton slung low across her hips. Above the waist it hangs open. One forearm lies across her chest and holds the two halves where they’d fall away, and holds them loosely, the cotton already slipping at the edge of her arm. Below her arm there’s a long bare stripe of her down the middle: the hollow of her throat, her breastbone, her stomach, her navel, the edge of the white cotton. Under that the skirt has swung mostly shut of its own weight, except where one knee has come forward through the gap, so that the line of a bare thigh runs out of the dress to the edge of the frame. Her other hand holds the white iPhone up beside her face, so it hides one eye, and its screen glows in the mirror like a second, smaller light. The eye he can see is looking straight out of the picture at him, and she’s biting the inside of her cheek, about to laugh and not letting herself yet.
His body answers before he has finished looking, all at once, and thirty-eight degrees is no help to him at all.

She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August. St. Nicholas Eve, at the end of my shift, low, at the pass: ‘Pecan came to see if you were here.’ Gave my Thursday to Hector — his girl’s due at Christmas. ‘Don’t argue with a baby.’ Says I look like the pie case at closing.

choices.text: Shut it. Erase it. Say nothing.
choices.key: Tuesday night, in the Anchor’s walk-in, you opened her third picture. You erased it and said nothing.
response: *Erase?* Yes. *Erased.*
He stands among the romaine with the phone shut in his fist until the fan in the ceiling cycles off, and the walk-in goes so quiet he can hear the eggs, nearly, and the fan comes on again.
He takes the case of eggs out with him, since somebody ought to bring something out of there, and sets it on the line by Rudy’s elbow. Rudy says thank you to the eggs.
At ten to one, with the last rack in, Gloria leans in at the pass with the pie server still in her hand and looks at him over the heat lamps. “You look like the pie case at closing, hon.”

s10a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:10 AM · MISSION STREET, THE GREYHOUND DEPOT BENCH
body: The Greyhound depot has its grate down for the night and one light left over its bench, a long tube in a wire cage that hums and makes everything under it look slightly seasick. Past it Mission Street runs downhill to the harbor without a car on it, the signals changing anyway. Jack is off at one. He has the bench and the light to himself, and his fingers still pruned from the sink, when the RAZR goes in his apron, and keeps going: a call.
“Keep me company,” Skye says. “I’m committing a crime.”

She’s in a laundromat in Studio City, she tells him, open all night, two blocks from her mother’s, with every light in the ceiling on and a TV bolted up in a corner selling knives to the empty chairs. She’s sitting cross-legged on a folding table in front of a front-loader, and going around in the front-loader, in the suds, is the preacher’s daughter’s dress.
“Wardrobe thinks it’s at the cleaners,” she says. “I’m a woman of my word. Approximately. I *am* the cleaners.”
“Your mother’s building doesn’t have a laundry room?”

“My mother’s building has a laundry room. My mother’s building also has my mother.” Something on her end clanks, a lid or a door. “It’s cotton from 1962, Jack. If it shrinks, I’m going to jail. Talk to me.”
“About what?”
“Anything that isn’t a dress. Your shift. Who came in. Give me one.”

So he gives her the man who eats his pie point-last, half an hour, a fork in one hand and the sports page in the other, and hasn’t touched the crust yet. She approves of him. She wants to know what he does with the crust. Jack doesn’t know. “Find out,” she says. “That’s the whole man. The crust.”

She isn’t sleeping tonight anyway, she tells him. At ten she has to be on a dock in Burbank with the rest of the cast for a picture, in sundresses, in December, pretending it’s June. She’ll sleep in the makeup chair. “They’re very gentle with a sleeping face,” she says. “It can’t do anything for anybody.”

He asks about the take, and she tells him. They kept the dry one. Take six, the one with no tears in it, is the one going to the network. “The director told the producer it was his idea,” she says. “He’s told it three times today. It gets better every time. By Friday he’ll have been out in the rain with me, holding my hand.”
Somebody at the agency sent the test to her mother as a file, and her mother watched it at the kitchen table on her laptop, with the legal pad. One note.
Skye clears her throat and becomes the legal pad: yellow, ruled, faintly let down by everyone it has ever met. “*Tired.*” A pause, for the pen. “Underlined.”
He laughs on the bench, and she lets him, and then she says, “She circled it, too,” and goes straight on to the lint trap.

body.text: “She said I looked tired,” Skye says. “I said I *was* tired. That was the note.”
body.else: “I *was* tired,” Skye says. “It was eleven at night in a rainstorm with a roof on it. Tired was the job.”

body.text: “Where were you,” she says, “when you opened it? The truth.” “A walk-in cooler. With the lettuce.” “And you said it was a problem.” On her end the washer slows, and starts up again faster. “Good. I like being a problem in a lettuce room.”

“You said don’t give it back.” “I said a lot of things.” “You said *no, don’t*. I heard the *don’t*.” The washer goes into its spin, a whine climbing down the line at him. “So I’m washing it for you. That’s romance.”

“You didn’t write back.” “I was at work.” “Mm.” She talks about the dress while it washes, as a dress: the cotton, the collar that stands up under the jaw, the buttons covered in the same white cloth, the wardrobe woman who counted them out on Monday and is going to count them back in. She has a good deal to say about the collar.
“You should know my mother was in the next room,” she says. “Watching the news. She was arguing with the weatherman. I could hear her through the door being right.”

body: At twenty past one the washer lets go of it and she moves it, wet and heavy, into a dryer; he hears her grunt with it. She sets the dial on low and reads it back to him twice to be sure.
“So,” she says. “How was your holy day? That’s a real thing you said to me in a car.”

body.text: “I went at noon.” “On three hours of sleep. On a Tuesday. On *purpose*.” “It’s a holy day.” “I know. You said.”
“I went at five-thirty.” “Was there singing?” “There’s always singing.” “Did you sing?” “Everybody sings that one.”
“I slept through it.” “Is that bad?” “It’s bad.” “Like a ticket?” “Like a confession.”

body: “I’ve still got it on me. You write like a doctor.” He can hear her turn her hand to the light. “The Immaculate Conception. That’s the Jesus one. The virgin thing.”

Half the parish at St. Brigid’s gets that one wrong. “It’s his mother,” Jack says. “Our Lady. That she was conceived without — that she started out clean. Without the stain, from the first second.” He has this part the way he has his own phone number. “Gina got it wrong on a test in sixth grade, and Nonna didn’t speak to the nuns for a month.”
“What stain?”
“The one everybody starts out with. Adam’s. It comes off at the font.” The bench is cold through his jeans. “She never had it to begin with.”
“Before she was born?”
“From the first second there was a her.”

body.text: And he gives her what the priest said, as near as he can get it. The angel doesn’t say *you will be*. He says *full of grace* like it’s already done, and in Luke’s Greek it is: a perfect participle, done and still done. She was graced before she’d said yes to anything. Before she’d done a single thing.

body: On her end a change machine pays somebody out in quarters, a long clatter, and stops.
“Must be nice,” Skye says.

choices.text: “It’s not just her. It’s the idea that you’re worth something before you’ve done anything. That part’s for everybody.”
response: “It’s not just her,” Jack says. “It’s the idea that you’re worth something before you’ve done anything. That part’s for everybody.”
On her end the dryer goes around. He gives it one turn, and another, under the hum of the cage light.
“Huh,” Skye says. And then she’s telling him about the collar, and whether a collar can shrink on its own, out of spite.

At a quarter to two the dryer stops, and she opens it, and he can hear her not breathing. Then: “It *lived*. Jack. It’s the same size. It’s a *miracle*.” Something rustles; she’s holding it up to the lights. “Is that a holy-day thing?”
She tells him how you fold a dress from 1962 so it never finds out it’s been anywhere.
Before she lets him go she says she’s up north on Thursday. “A test. A real one. With a pencil.” A breath on the line. “Don’t ask me how I feel about it.” And she hangs up first.

choices.text: “I’m the other kind. I’m the one in the line on Saturday afternoons.”
response: “I’m the other kind,” Jack says. “I’m the one in the line on Saturday afternoons.”
“Every Saturday?” Skye says. “What do you *do* all week?”
“You’ve met me.”
She laughs at that longer than it deserves, with the dryer going around behind her.

body: He got in off Mission Street a little after two with the phone still warm in his hand and slept like a dropped coat, and at twenty past eight he’s going down the fourth-floor hall in yesterday’s Carhartt with his toothbrush, past the east-stair door and the EXIT sign and the red handle under it, which he gives a long look.

body.text: The fourth-floor lounge at twenty past eight is the microwave counting down somebody’s oatmeal and the squeak of a dry-erase marker. Margot is at the whiteboard in black, with a coffee already going cold on the sill beside her. She has taken UNEXPLAINED CITRUS off the top of the board with the side of her fist — a gray smear is all that’s left of it — and left Laney’s pink column alone. In its place, in her capitals:

body.title: 4th-floor lounge whiteboard
body.text:
FIRE ALARMS (5): CASE CLOSED.
SUSPECT: PRUITT, D. (ASLEEP).
WITNESS: COSTIGAN, J. (UNEXPLAINED).

TIGER — A COUNT (L.P.): MORE.

Doug Pruitt comes in for cereal in the hoodie and his green Crocs and stops dead in front of the board with the box of Lucky Charms against his chest. He reads it with his lips moving, top to bottom, and back up to his own name.
“Dude,” he says. “Am I *famous*?”
“You’re a *sleepwalker*, Douglas,” says Margot.
Doug considers this with everything he has. “…*Rad*.”

“October the thirteenth,” Margot tells him, “you came out of the wrong fire door in what was left of a typhoon and walked through a puddle to the ankle without breaking stride. I had you down as *indifferent to weather*.” She looks at the board. “I was wrong about the adjective.”
“Does that mean I did all *five*?”

“It means you’re asleep at four in the morning with your eyes open, Douglas, during finals.” She hands him back the Lucky Charms, which he has set down beside her coffee. “Eat something. Go to bed at a Christian hour.”

Kevin comes in behind Jack with his mug, reads the board over the top of it, and says, “Huh. Parasomnia. I had him down for sleep apnea,” and looks at Doug with real medical tenderness, and at the WITNESS line, and at Jack, and goes to fill the mug.
Margot caps the marker and turns around and looks at Jack in the doorway with his toothbrush. “The witness,” she says, “may wish to make a statement.”

Every time the door of 420 moves, it jingles. Kevin has hung a Christmas bell on the inside knob on a loop of dental floss — mint, waxed — and inside, in the hoodie, Doug is asking the room in general why the door is festive.

Kevin is in the doorway in the navy quarter-zip with the orgo text under his arm, on his way out, and he has already done all of it. “Priya at seven,” he tells Jack. “In her doorway, in her retainer. The health center gets a call the Monday after finals. The bell stays.”
“Because you’re a flight risk,” Kevin says over his shoulder. “Non-REM parasomnia. Textbook. Stress plus sleep debt, and it’s finals.”
From inside: “Is that *bad*?”
“It’s festive,” says Kevin.

Doug comes to the door in the hoodie, setting off the bell, with his hair flat on one side. “Dude,” he says to Jack, warmly. “I don’t remember *any* of it. Kevin says you were *there*.” He shakes Jack’s hand, toothbrush and all. “Thanks, dude.” He goes back in to his cereal, jingling.
“The raid boss is nine feet tall,” Kevin says. “I got a full description at breakfast. He doesn’t remember telling me.”
Then Kevin looks at Jack straight. Not at the blazer, which is on a hanger, or the pass, which is in a drawer. At Jack. “Why were *you* in the hall at four, Jack?”
“On the lawn Saturday I erased a question mark next to your name,” Kevin says. “I’m drawing it back in.”
In Jack’s pocket the RAZR buzzes, and his hand is on it before the second buzz. Kevin’s eyes go to the pocket, and come back up.

The fourth-floor lounge at twenty past eight is Priya’s laminator, warming up on the table. She is making NO SHOES IN HALLWAYS (FIRE CODE) again, a size larger, for the lounge. UNEXPLAINED CITRUS — FLOORS 2–4 is still at the top of Margot’s whiteboard, with THE CATHOLICS still listed under it as the suspects.

body.title: Priya’s new laminate, the lounge door
body.text:
NO SHOES IN HALLWAYS (FIRE CODE)
THIS INCLUDES THE LOUNGE.
THIS INCLUDES CROCS.
— Priya, RA, 401
Doug Pruitt is at the counter under the window in the hoodie, eating Lucky Charms out of the box with his fingers. He’s barefoot. There is grass on the soles of his feet.

“Dude,” Doug says, when he sees Jack. “I had the *craziest* dream. You were in it.” He eats a marshmallow horseshoe. “You had a *jacket* on. And there was a raid boss in the elevator, and you were all, like, *I’ll tell him*.” He points a horseshoe at Jack. “Did you tell him?”

The laminator takes a sheet in and thinks about it. Priya looks up from it at Doug’s feet, and at the grass on them, and opens her mouth, and closes it, and feeds the laminator another sheet. “Five alarms, Costigan,” she tells Jack instead. “The fire marshal knows my first name. He uses it.”
Doug looks at Jack, puzzled and friendly. “Why’d you have a jacket on?”

choices.text: “I was up with a sick friend.”
response: “I was up with a sick friend.”

response.text: “Douglas *is* the sick friend,” says Margot, and picks up her cold coffee, and drinks it anyway.
“Your friends get sick at noon,” Kevin says. “I’ve met them.” He goes off down the hall with the orgo book, and behind him 420’s door jingles shut.
Doug thinks about it. His face falls. “Dude,” he says. “Was it *me*?”

response: “I was out.”

response.text: “I know,” says Margot. She leaves the WITNESS line up.
“I know you were out,” Kevin says. He pulls the door to, and the bell jingles behind it, and he goes to class.
“Out where?” says Doug. “Like, *outside*?”
“Like outside.”
Doug nods slowly, a man in the presence of mystery. “…Rad.”
Margot looks at him over the capped marker. Then she leaves the line up and takes her coffee to class.
Kevin waits about as long as a polite man waits for an answer, and then he goes to class.
Doug doesn’t notice. He’s already explaining the raid boss to Priya, who has stopped laminating to listen with an expression of growing professional concern.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Tuesday at four in the morning she opened 305 before I knocked. Wednesday: FIRE ALARMS (5): CASE CLOSED. SUSPECT: PRUITT, D. (ASLEEP). WITNESS: COSTIGAN, J. (UNEXPLAINED).

body: The last seminar gets low winter sun straight down the long table from the west windows, so bright on the wood that half the table sits squinting like card players. Yusuf’s chair is the third one down on the window side, empty. Caleb has learned.

Hale comes in at one o’clock exactly, in a dark jacket Jack hasn’t seen before, pressed, with nothing on either cuff. He sits down. “Mr. Noorzai flies back tonight,” he says. “His chair has been very patient. Let us be the same.”

He spends the last hour where he spent the first one, in September — *prove to me you have a soul* — only this time he argues for it himself and makes them take it apart, and when Caleb takes it apart with Hume, Hale tells him that was very nearly a sentence.

Lena says nothing. She sits across from Jack with her pen capped and her notebook shut and the sun on her hands, and listens, and for an hour she doesn’t open her mouth: not to Caleb, not to Hale, not when Hale walks right up to the edge of an argument she has been winning since September and stands there waiting for her.
At two o’clock Hale looks at the clock, and then down the table. “Miss Broussard has said nothing for an hour,” he says mildly. “Note the date.”
“I’m saving it for Wednesday, Professor.”

She smiles when she says it. Her face is very bright, and looks washed, recently and hard, in cold water: the face of somebody who has been handed something too big to carry home. She meets Jack’s eyes across the table, and uncaps her pen, and caps it again.
“Wednesday the sixteenth,” Hale says. “Two at a time, each of you defending the other’s best argument, with me in the way. You know that much. Here is what you don’t know.”

“By Friday each of you will email me which argument of the other’s you intend to defend. Choose the best one. If you choose a weak one in order to win, I shall know.” He looks down the table at the pairs. “So will they.”

He picks up his coffee. “Tomorrow the President accepts a prize for peace, nine days after sending thirty thousand more young men to a war. He will have to say something clever about that, and he will. Read it. One of you will want to quote it at me next Wednesday.” He drinks. “Resist.”
At the door, getting into his coat, he says to the hall: “I shall have the town to myself again in a week.”

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know.

s13.slug: WEDNESDAY · 11:20 PM · THE BRICK, 8TH FLOOR, THE 24-HOUR READING ROOM

body.text: Brick. Eighth floor. We have to pick. Bring your margins. —L.

body: On finals-eve hours the eighth floor of the Brick doesn’t close, and at twenty past eleven thirty people are up here doing their best impression of people who are going to pass. Under the long windows the radiators knock — iron on iron, somewhere down in the pipe, every couple of minutes, with no rhythm a person could tap along to. A girl at the far end of the long table is asleep with her cheek on *Gray’s Anatomy* and a highlighter still uncapped in her fist.

Lena has the end of the long table by the windows, staked out with her coat on one chair and the Loeb on the other. At the carrel just past the end of the table, Kevin Tran is in a pair of headphones the size of earmuffs with a rubber-banded block of orgo flashcards, mouthing reagents. He lifts his chin at Jack and goes back to a carbocation.
“He was here first,” Lena says. “Don’t let him quiz you. He bites.”
Jack sits. He puts the RAZR on the table, face down, and leaves his palm on top of it.
Lena looks at his hand on it. She takes her LG out of her pocket and sets it down on the table beside his, face up, with the little screen lit and nothing on it but the time, and uncaps her pen.

The papers come out of her bag in two stacks: his semester on the left and hers on the right, every page with the other one’s ink down the margins. Two kinds of red. Hers is a felt-tip and goes through to the next page, so every paper of his carries a ghost of her on its back; his is a Bic and gives out in the middle of words.

“Hale wants it by Friday,” she says. “Which of mine you’ll defend. Which of yours I will.” She drops into Hale — the vowels, the eyebrows, the long-suffering chin. “*Choose the best one. If you choose a weak one to win, I shall know.*” And back into herself. “And I will personally know before he does.”
“Twenty minutes each,” Jack says. “Back to back. In front of him.”
“In front of him, and in front of me, and I’ll be sitting right there next to you making faces.” She uncaps the pen. “So pick well.”
“Take the luck one,” Jack says. “You wrote on it that it was my best. In red.”

“In September. I’d just lost to you. I was being gracious, it’s a Southern illness.” She turns *That the Lucky Man Owes Nothing* face up and looks at her own handwriting on it like a relative she’s embarrassed by. “It’s a good paper. It’s the paper a smart boy writes so he never has to owe anybody anything. You argued it like it was yours.”
“It was mine.”
“That’s my objection.” She puts it on the floor.
“The leaving one. Hale liked it.”

“Hale said you argued for leaving like a man who’s never been allowed to. I am not standing up in front of that man and defending *that*. He’d look at me the whole twenty minutes.” The leaving paper goes on the floor. “And don’t say the dead.”
“The dead are beyond harm—”
“You *lost* that one, Costigan. To me. I’m not defending my own victim.”
“You’re supposed to pick one of mine, not throw them all on the floor.”
“I’m clearing the field.” The paper on the dead goes down on top of the others. “It’s a process of elimination. It’s very Thomist. Sit still.”
At the next carrel Kevin turns a flashcard over, and over again, and then lifts one side of the headphones off his ear and holds the card up at Jack. “Backside attack,” he says. “Go.”
“I’m a philosophy major.”
“So that’s a no.” The headphone goes back on.

She goes into the middle of his stack like she knew where it was all along, and pulls out the paper from October, and lays it under the lamp beside the two phones. His first sentence. And beside it in the margin, in her capitals, hard enough that the paper still has the dent: *THEN WHAT DID YOU TELL HIM?*
She doesn’t read the margin. She reads the sentence. “*A man knows his own heart by what he says yes to.*”

“That one,” Lena says. “It’s your best. You were wrong about everything else that night. Not that.” She taps the sentence with the cap of her pen. “I’ve been looking for the hole in it since October. I can’t find it. I’ve checked.”
Under Jack’s palm the phone has gone warm from his hand, and his fingers close on it.
“Now you,” she says, and pushes her own stack over to his side. “Pick mine. And don’t pick to win.”
“And not the loyalty one,” she adds, as his hand goes toward it. “I quoted Ruth at him. You can’t stand up and defend Ruth in front of Hale. He’ll do the Book of Common Prayer at you and you’ll cry.”

He goes through them anyway. Luck, from the other side. Loyalty, and Peter in John six — *Lord, to whom shall we go?* — with his Bic giving up in the middle of *whom*. Monica, asking to be remembered at the altar. The promise paper, which she argued without believing a sentence of, and which doesn’t read that way. And under all of them, the ones she never wrote down — said across Hale’s table, or in a church courtyard one Sunday in August — and won.

choices.text: “A promise is made to a person, not to a reason.”
choices.key: At the Brick you chose the argument of Lena’s you’ll defend for Hale: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason.
response: “This one,” Jack says. “*A promise is made to a person, not to a reason.*”
Lena looks at the paper in his hand. “That’s the one I didn’t believe.”
“It doesn’t read that way.”

“That’s what makes it the *easy* one, Costigan. It reads like a winner.” She caps her pen. “You’re picking to win.” She lets him sit in that a moment, and then shrugs, Southern and final. “Fine. Defend it like you mean it. He’ll know if you don’t. So will I.”

choices.text: “The dead can be wronged, and therefore helped.”
choices.key: At the Brick you chose the argument of Lena’s you’ll defend for Hale: that the dead can be wronged, and therefore helped.
