For an hour and a half she has been taking his paper apart and putting it back together in her own order, in a whisper, with the cap of her pen for a pointer. Aristotle first, book two: *we become just by doing just things*. James second — faith without works. His own sentence last, where it belongs. It sounds different in New Orleans. It sounds like it might be true. He has her argument in front of him on a legal pad, and a page and a half of reasons for it in his own hand, and she has crossed out two of them as unworthy of her.

At half past twelve she made him do it for real — “Twenty minutes. I’m Hale. Go.” — and stopped him at three. “You said *I think*. Never say *I think* to that man. He’ll ask you how you know, and then he’ll ask you how you know *that*, and by the third one you won’t know your own name.” He started again. She let him go seven minutes the second time, and at the end of it she said, “Better,” and wrote something in her own margin he wasn’t allowed to see.
Now she has his paper again and is writing down the empty margin of it, the one she didn’t use in October. She doesn’t look up from it.
“He played it for me,” she says. “Tuesday night. After the holy day. In his garage.”
Her pen goes on to the end of the line it was on and stops there.
“It’s good, Jack.” She caps the pen. “It’s really good.”
Jack puts his own pen down on the legal pad.

That’s all she gives it. She turns the page over, and squares it on the stack, and when she looks over at him at last she is smiling — the smile of somebody owning up to an old sin in front of a witness.
“Come tonight,” she says. “Bastille. Tomorrow. Tonight — whatever it is after midnight.” She’s still smiling. “And whatever you do, don’t leave in the second chorus.”

journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. body.text: done. i didnt cry. launch ramp. 3

body: He’s on the 2:40 into town with the phone still open in his hand.

In daylight the far side of the harbor has a job. The sun is already low over the breakwater, the December kind that comes in sideways and finds everything, and it finds a boatyard behind chain-link with a hull up on stands and a man under it going at the bottom paint with a sander; the fuel dock, where the pump dings a little bell at every gallon for a trawler taking on diesel; a guy in rubber boots hosing down a deck and whistling through his teeth. The lamp over the lot is just a lamp on a pole. Across the water the Anchor is gray shingles on pilings with its sign switched off, nothing he’d look at twice.

The Saab is nosed up to the rail with the top down again. The rain is gone, and the rule is back. Skye is cross-legged on the trunk lid in a gray Marisol sweatshirt she must have bought today, the price tag still hanging off the cuff on its plastic thread, with a sleeve of No. 2 pencils in her lap and a sheet of scratch paper she wasn’t supposed to keep.
She holds the paper up in both hands as he comes across the lot, like a ticket that won.
“You kept it?”
“They said leave your scratch paper on the desk,” she says. “I didn’t. I’m a criminal now. It’s been a big week for me.”

He takes it. Both sides are long division going downhill, and in every margin there are circles cut into slices, twelve to a circle, most of them, some shaded in and some shaded twice. Halfway down the back there’s a seven in a quotient that ought to be a one, and he puts his thumb under it.
She puts her hand flat over the seven. “It’s handed in. I’m *free*.”
His eyes go to the price tag on her cuff. “The bookstore,” she says. “The kid at the register asked if I wanted a bag. That’s all he wanted out of me. Yes or no on a bag.”

“A room in the science building,” she says. “Forty of us. Eighteen, mostly. I was the old lady. They all had one pencil. I brought twelve.” She rattles the sleeve. “A proctor with a kitchen timer shaped like an egg. A clock on the wall you could *hear*. I’ve never been anyplace quiet enough to hear a clock.” She pulls her knees up under the sweatshirt. “And Jack. For two hours —”
She stops, to get it right.
“For two hours, not one person in that room looked at me. Forty people, and every one of them was looking at a fraction. Nobody needed my face. My face had the afternoon *off*.”

She lies back on the trunk lid with her arms flung out and the sun on her, and the pencils go rolling, and she laughs straight up at the sky. She sits up again. She can’t keep still. She’s up on her knees on the trunk, and then down off it, barefoot on the asphalt, and then back up, and the whole time she’s telling him — the girl beside her who chewed her pencil down to the metal, the boy who signed his name in cursive, the egg timer going off at the end and forty people letting out their air at once like a congregation sitting down — and he stands at the rail with her scratch paper and listens to all of it.
“Seven-twelfths came in,” she says, “and I said, *love what you’re doing*. I cast every one of them. I was extremely fair.”
“How’d you do?”

“I have *no idea*,” she says, and laughs. “They mail you a number. In January. I don’t even know what the number’s out of.” She points a pencil back up Mission, toward campus and the room in the science building. “And I read every one of them, Jack, I couldn’t help it. The girl by the window is going to be a vet. The boy with the cursive is going to marry her, and she has no idea.” The pencil comes down. “Not one of them read me back.”
“That sounds lonely.”

“It was *heaven*.” She lies back on the trunk again, with the sweatshirt hiked up and the sun on her stomach. “Two hours in a room full of people, and I was furniture. Write that down. I want it on my stone.”
“They read the roll off the paperwork,” she says, with her eyes shut in the sun. “Off the application.”
“And?”
“A name I don’t use. Nobody turned around.” She takes a pencil out of the sleeve and puts it behind her ear.
“What’s on the paperwork?”
“Ask me in a different daylight.”
“You said you wanted me here,” she says, with her face still turned up into the sun. “This is here.”
She turns her head on the trunk lid to look at him. “Do they know yet? Your everybody.” “No.” “Okay.” She shuts her eyes again in the sun.
He sits on the back bumper below her, and she sits up and puts her bare feet in his lap, cold as the harbor, sand on them from somewhere, and he holds one in each hand to warm it.
“What are you doing tonight?”
“A friend’s playing a song,” Jack says. “Open mic. I said I’d stay to the end.”
She nods, like that’s a reasonable thing for a person to have promised. “I’m up here tonight. At the house.” She has never said where the house is, and she doesn’t now. “Do your thing. After?”
*Keep her in the daylight.* Here she is in it, with a pencil behind her ear and her bare feet on a trunk lid in December, and it is easy.
She leans down off the trunk and kisses him, short, in front of the fuel dock and the man with the hose and God and everybody, and she tastes of pencil.

response: “I’m going to want you after,” Jack says.
“Then call,” Skye says. “You never call. I always call.” She takes the pencil from behind her ear and points it at him, the eraser end. “*Call.*”
“Nobody looking suits you,” Jack says.
“Write that on my stone too,” she says, and pulls the sleeve of the new sweatshirt down over her hand, price tag and all.
“Did you cast the proctor?”

She did. She gives him the proctor right there on the trunk lid: a disappointed aunt from Barstow in a cardigan with a tissue up the sleeve, who set the egg timer like she was setting it for all of their funerals and had given up on every one of them by the second page, and was very nice about it. “*Pencils down, sweethearts. You did what you could.*”

s14a.slug: THURSDAY · 4:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: CNN has been running Oslo since four in the morning, and at half past four in the afternoon it’s still on the Fishbowl’s TV with the sound down to one bar: the President at a lectern in a hall full of Norwegians in evening clothes, giving the same speech again to a lounge that is mostly studying. Outside the glass the Lagoon has gone gold. Margot has the armchair and the transcript, printed off the White House website and already red in the margins. Lena is on the couch with her knees up and a Greek lexicon she no longer needs open on them, out of habit.

Yusuf is back. He flew in last night, and he’s at the end of the couch where he sat for West Point, with one hand on the arm beside him, holding it. When Jack comes in he takes the hand away. “My mother says thank you,” he says, low, when Jack sits. “For the stairs. The other stairs.”

Margot reads off the transcript without any expression at all. “‘Evil does exist in the world. A non-violent movement could not have halted Hitler’s armies. Negotiations cannot convince al Qaeda’s leaders to lay down their arms.’” She looks up. “Costigan.”
“I agree with every word,” Jack says, and hears himself. “I agree with every word a Democrat said in Norway. I’m going to have to call my father, and neither one of us is going to know what to say.”

“‘I face the world as it is,’” Margot reads. She lowers the page. “He accepted a *peace* prize for a *surge*. Every man who ever sent anybody to a war said evil exists, Costigan. It’s the first sentence of the genre. The question is who gets to decide which villagers are the cost.”
“He gave the conditions himself,” Lena says from the couch. “Last resort. Proportion. Spare the civilians. Aquinas would grade it a B and ask him to name the week in eight years we met all three.”
“You can’t grade a war by the week.”
“Watch me, Costigan.”
“Dorothy Day would’ve sent the prize money to the Catholic Worker,” she says, “and the medal back to Oslo. Postage due.”

Laney puts her head in at the Fishbowl door with her hair up in a towel. “Lena. Seven-thirty. I am doing your hair whether you want it done or not.” She sees the TV. “Is he *still* talking?” And she’s gone.
Yusuf has been watching the President with his hands between his knees. “My brother’s learning stairs,” he says. “I’d like the speech to be right.”
On the screen the President goes on, a bar too low to hear. Margot lets the transcript down onto her knee.

choices.text: Agree with the President out loud.
response: “He’s right,” Jack says, to the room, and to Yusuf. “There’s evil in the world, and some people go and stand between it and everybody else. You can hate that it’s true. It’s still true.”
Lena looks at him over her knees. “Write the date down, Margot.”
“I’m not giving you the satisfaction of ink,” says Margot.
“The stairs,” Jack says. “What are they like?”

Yusuf tells him. Parallel bars first, in a long room with a mirror at the end of it so you can watch yourself do it wrong. Then a walker, which Tariq hates and has named. Then the stairs: eleven of them, a rail on each side, a therapist one step below him the whole way. “Monday he did all eleven,” Yusuf says. “My mother counted them on the phone, out loud, to my father, who was standing right there.” He almost smiles. “My father said he could count.”

choices.text: “I need Margot to tell me I’m wrong so I can feel normal.”
response: “I need Margot to tell me I’m wrong so I can feel normal.”
“You’re wrong,” says Margot, turning a page.
“Thank you,” says Jack. “I feel much better.”

journal.title: Yusuf (PHIL 9H)
journal.text: Fremont. Engineer. Fasting for Ramadan through a ninety-minute seminar and funnier than all of us. Broke the fast with his people on Mission Street and fed me till I couldn’t stand. Father on the NUMMI line since ’85. Brother Tariq interprets for the Army in Helmand and calls on Sundays. The day of Fort Hood I asked if Tariq was okay. He’s not in Texas. Friday morning he called: he’s fine, and he said don’t watch the news. Yusuf watched the news. At Hale’s table a man asked him what Muslims think. He’d like one week where nobody asks. His nineteenth, at Bastille, with a candle in a scone. He watched the memorial Tuesday. Standing up. I didn’t ask. The night of the West Point speech: ‘You left the first time. My father watched you leave. If you’re going to come, stay.’ His brother Tariq — an IED in Helmand. Alive. Germany. I went after him. We sat on the east stairs. Back for finals the night before Oslo. Tariq’s learning stairs. He’d like the speech to be right.

s15.slug: THURSDAY · 9:10 PM · CAFÉ BASTILLE, MISSION STREET
body: At ten past nine Bastille is string lights and steam: the front windows have fogged to the height of a man, so that Mission Street outside is only headlights going by in a blur. The sign-up board by the register is full to the bottom. On the stool at the front a girl with a ukulele is finishing badly, which is taking some time, because she keeps finding one more verse about a boy named Tanner who doesn’t text back. Julian is seventh, in yellow chalk.

Half of Delgado has come out for Julian. Margot is on the bench along the brick wall with her red Dymo badge — PRESS — stuck to the front of her black coat and a reporter’s notebook open on her knee; she reviews the open mic for the *Tide*. Kevin is beside her with a hot chocolate. Yusuf, back from Fremont since last night, has the far end of the bench with his coat still on; he has been on planes all week.

Theo is at the counter in the camel coat with an espresso, on a stool by himself. When Julian comes through the tables with the guitar case, Theo turns on his stool to watch him pass. “Julian. Pitch it to me. Logline. A man, a stool, a Thursday —”
“It’s four minutes, Theo.”
“Four minutes. Bold. Kubrick would’ve cut it to three.”
“Let the man sing,” Kevin says, low, from the bench, and Theo lifts his cup to Kevin in a toast and drinks it.

Margot, when Jack goes past the bench, doesn’t look up from her notebook. “I’ve been asked to be kind,” she says. “By Laney. So it’s a threat.” Kevin considers Jack across the top of his hot chocolate. “You look like a man who’s been up since Tuesday,” he says. “Clinically.”

Laney is at the front table in a red sweater with a sequined reindeer on it, polite as a church bulletin to Julian’s face. “It is going to be *beautiful*, Julian.” Julian thanks her and goes to tune. The moment his back is turned Laney swivels in her chair and points at the empty chair on Lena’s left — Julian’s, with his scarf still over the back of it, because Julian will be on the stool. “Sit, fireman. *There*.”

Jack sits there. Laney reaches across Lena for the scarf and folds it into a square on her knee, like a flag at a funeral. Across the room, at the counter, Theo catches her eye and gives her a nod so small it barely moves his head.

Lena is in a green dress and her boots, with her coat over the chair behind her, and in front of her on the table there’s a tea and a paper napkin already folded twice. She looks at him when he sits down. “You came.” She tips her head at the chalkboard. “He’s seventh.” A fold in the napkin. On the stool the ukulele has found another verse. “Somebody should tell her about Tanner.” Another fold. “Did you send Hale yours?”
“Tomorrow.”

“It’s *due* tomorrow.” She looks at him over the napkin. “I sent mine at seven this morning. I put the subject line in Latin so he’d know I wasn’t scared of him.” She turns the napkin over. “I was a little scared of him.”

Laney leans across her, all reindeer, and puts one red fingernail on the table in front of Jack. “Phone stays in the pocket,” she says, sweet as pie. “Four minutes. I will be watching you like a pageant mom watches a judge.” Jack puts his hand over the pocket of the Carhartt, and she sits back, satisfied.
The ukulele finishes. People clap for it, generously. Julian takes the stool.

He tunes. It takes as long as it takes, and he doesn’t make a joke about it; he keeps his head down by the sound hole. People settle. Somebody at the back shushes somebody, and the somebody shushes back.
Before he starts he looks out at the front table — at Lena, and then, for no longer than that, at Jack — and then down at the floor in front of the stool, and leans in to the mic.
“This one’s new,” he says. “It’s called ‘Magdalena.’”
Under the table Jack’s hand takes hold of his own knee.

It starts low, fingerpicked: a figure that climbs four notes and comes back down to where it began, and climbs again, in a key that sounds like the inside of a church on a weekday. The first verse is a woman up before the light — a garden, a stone, a dark that hasn’t made up its mind to be morning. Jack knows the story; anybody knows it who has sat through an Easter octave in Youngstown. A woman who goes to a grave in the dark to do the last thing she can do for somebody, and finds it open, and runs. Julian sings it with his eyes on the floor in front of the stool.
*You were up before the light, and you ran the whole way in the dark,* he sings, *and you didn’t know him till he said your name.*
His voice isn’t big, and he doesn’t push it. Where the line goes higher than he can comfortably go he lets the guitar take it, and comes in again under it.
At the counter Theo sets his cup down in its saucer, and it doesn’t make a sound.

The chorus is a man outside a door. He can’t get in. He can’t play what they’re playing in there, he doesn’t know the words they know; all he has is her name, and he stands outside with it — *I’m outside the door, saying it every way I know.* And at the end of it, every time, the name.
Jack sits in the chair Laney put him in, holding on to his own knee, and listens to another man say it.
On the bench Margot caps her pen. The notebook stays open on her knee.
The second verse starts, and Lena isn’t watching the stage.

Jack can feel it on the side of his face. At the edge of his eye she has turned a little in her chair, and the folded napkin has gone still under her fingers, and she is watching him hear it. Not Julian. Him. Her hand goes up to the medal at her throat and holds it.
On Lena’s other side Laney’s hand comes across the table, without any fuss at all, and finds Lena’s free one, and keeps it.

The verse is the gardener. She takes him for the man who cuts the grass. She asks him where they’ve put the body, so she can go and get it, and he doesn’t argue with her or explain anything; he only says her name. Julian plays that part quieter, so the room has to lean in for it.
Jack knows what she says back to the gardener. She answers him with a name too. It isn’t in the song.
And the song goes back around to the door, and the man outside it, and the second chorus starts to come.

response: He turns his head and meets her eyes. They’re dry.

They look at each other through the second chorus, with a good man singing her name at the front of the room and the room listening to him do it. She doesn’t look away first. He doesn’t either. The table is quiet.

At the bridge she turns to the stage, and on the table Laney’s hand tightens on hers. Jack looks at the stage too, then, at Julian with his eyes shut, and the last chorus comes around and goes, and the name with it, and he doesn’t look at her again until it’s over.

response: He keeps his face on the stage.

He watches Julian: the calluses on the hand that holds the chord, the Timex on the wrist, the eyes shut on the high part of the second chorus. A good man, singing. And the whole time, through the chorus and the bridge and the last verse, he can feel her watching the side of his face, and he gives her nothing to see but the side of his face. At the bridge he hears her breathe in, once, and hold it, and let it go when the chorus comes back.

s15a.slug: THURSDAY · 9:40 PM · CAFÉ BASTILLE, THE COUNTER
body: It ends on the name, and on the guitar after the name, and then nothing for a moment — and then the room applauds the way a small room applauds something it didn’t see coming, all at once, a little late, and for longer than it means to. Somebody at the back whistles.

Julian says, “Thanks,” into the mic, and then, “That’s all I’ve got,” and gets down off the stool with the guitar by the neck. People touch his shoulder as he comes back through the tables — the ukulele girl, a man in a bike helmet — and he thanks each of them and looks a little alarmed by it.
Lena has her hands in her lap. Laney still has one of them.

choices.text: Find Julian at the counter. “It’s good, Julian.”
response: Julian is at the counter by the tip jar, laying the guitar down in its case like he’s putting a child to bed. Jack goes and stands next to him.
“It’s good, Julian.”
Julian looks up from the case. “You stayed.” And then, quietly, looking past Jack’s shoulder at the front table, where Lena is sitting with her hands in her lap: “She wanted you here.”
He snaps the latches shut, one, two, three.
Jack’s out the door before ten, with the Carhartt half on. On his way past, Laney catches the sleeve of it.
“Where are you *going*?”
“Out.”

Mission Street is cold and dry and lit to the end. Through a clear patch somebody has wiped in Bastille’s steamed window, as he walks east, Theo is at the counter in the camel coat, turned around on his stool, watching him go.
“It’s good,” Jack says to her.
“I know.”

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus.

journal.text: Julian Park-Ellis. The guitar guy from the Lighthouse stairs. Plays Bastille Thursdays. Wrote a song called “Fresno.” Plays it once a month. A handshake you’d trust with anything. Sunday he came to the nine o’clock with Lena. Didn’t receive. Had the Sanctus by ear by the end. Picked Lena up at twenty to twelve for the vampires, straight from Bastille. Friday he brought her juk in his mother’s thermos and asked her what she’d go to jail for, and listened to all of it. Thursday at Bastille: it’s called ‘Magdalena.’ It’s good. ‘You stayed. She wanted you here.’

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window.

s16a.slug: THURSDAY · 10:16 PM · THE SAAB, MISSION STREET → DEL PLAYA
body: Eleven minutes later the Saab comes down Mission with its top down in the cold, the only car on the street, and noses in at the curb under the drugstore’s glare. She’s in the gray Marisol sweatshirt from the launch ramp, with the price tag gone from the cuff, and her feet are bare on the pedals.

He gets in. She doesn’t put it in gear. She looks at him, at his face in that light, while the signal at the corner goes green and yellow and red and green again over an empty street, and she reads it to the bottom. When she’s done she reaches across him and turns the heater over to the floor on his side, onto his boots, and puts the car in gear.

At the first light he takes the RAZR out of the Carhartt and holds the red key down. It plays its little falling chime, four notes going downstairs, and the screen goes black in his hand. Skye hears it. Her eyes go to his hand and back to the light, which is green, and she drives.

*Two in the morning, and a car, and nobody who knows where you are.* Father Osei said it on Saturday, through the linen. It’s a quarter past ten, and it’s a car, and nobody knows where he is, and seven hours ago he had her in daylight on a trunk lid with pencils rolling off it and it was easy. He knows which kind of hour this is. He sits back in the seat and lets her drive it.
Mission runs out at the Grove. At the last light, with the eucalyptus black on both sides of the road, Skye says, with her eyes on the road.
“I told you I don’t take people home.”
“I remember.”
“I’ve decided I want to.”

She turns west into Las Olas. Del Playa on a Thursday night at half past ten is music out of three houses at once, a couch on somebody’s lawn with two people asleep on it sitting up, a kid on a roof with a flashlight looking for something in the gutter. She doesn’t park on it. She takes the alley behind, and stops the Saab nose-in beside a trash can with a house number painted on it in nail polish, and they go around to the front through a side yard grown over with ice plant.

The house is two stories of shingle gone silver, with a porch across the front that leans toward the street like it’s trying to hear something. On the porch stands a surfboard rack built out of two-by-fours, with no surfboards on it. “They’re in Baja,” she says. “The boys. Sol’s in LA. It’s just me and the darkroom.”

Inside, off the hall, there’s a door with a towel rolled along the bottom of it and a red bulb over the frame, unlit, and a smell of vinegar coming out from under the towel. She goes past it and starts up the stairs ahead of him, barefoot.
Halfway up she turns around on the stair, above him, with her hand on the rail. “This is where I’m going to live,” she says. “In January. When I’m normal.”

s17.slug: THURSDAY · 10:40 PM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: Her room is lit by its window. She strung the Christmas lights around the frame herself — there’s a thumbtack every foot, and where she ran out of thumbtacks, gaff tape — and the left half of the strand is out, so the right half throws red and green and a white gone yellow down onto a mattress on a low frame under the sill, and the left half throws nothing at all. The window is open a few inches at the bottom. Through it come the surf at the foot of the bluff and somebody’s stereo three houses down, taking turns.

A clothes rack on casters is most of the furniture: flannels, a black dress in plastic, a parka for somewhere colder than California, and under it a row of boots lined up heel to heel. Scripts in rubber bands stand in a stack against the wall, the brads winking. By the bed there’s a jar of beach glass, green and brown, with one blue piece set on top last. There’s nothing on the walls. “Walls are for leases,” she says, when she sees him look. Nothing in this room knows anything about him but her.

On the sill, under the working half of the lights, a paperback O’Connor lies open at the end of the story with its spine broken in two places, and he knows the margin before he’s close enough to read it: her capitals, and one hard line of Sharpie through CON.

On the back of the door, on the one hook, in a dry cleaner’s bag with a paper collar around the hanger, hangs a white dress with a collar that stands up and forty buttons down the front. “The top leaks,” Skye says. “I wasn’t leaving it in the car. Wardrobe gets it Monday.” He knows the dress. His body knows it faster than he does.

She turns him by the shoulders and peels the Carhartt down off his arms and hangs it on the hook over the dress, so the dress is gone under brown canvas that smells of the Anchor’s fryer. She looks at the white iPhone in her hand, at the time on it, and drops it into one of the boots under the rack.
“No clock tonight,” she says.
She kicks a heap of clothes in under the rack with one bare foot. “Housekeeping,” she says.
“You’re the first person up those stairs,” she says, “who wasn’t Sol, or a surfer looking for a towel.” And then she turns around.

She starts where the turnout left off. The sweatshirt comes off over her head and lands on the jar of beach glass, and there’s nothing under it, and she’s already at his shirt buttons from the top, fast, and shoving the shirt off his shoulders, and the undershirt after it, so they’re skin to skin standing up in the middle of the room in the light off the window, and cold for about the length of a breath. She walks him backward by his belt loops till the frame of the bed catches him behind the knees, and he goes down onto the mattress, and she comes down with him, and the frame creaks under them.

It’s the first time they’ve been lying down. Every other time there was a car around them, or a trailer bench, or a gearshift, or somebody’s knuckles on a door. Here there’s a mattress and a window and her weight, and she puts all of it on him.

She’s warm everywhere he’d have guessed and in places he wouldn’t — the backs of her arms, the small of her back — and cold only where the window gets her: one shoulder blade, the side of her face, which he warms with his hand. Her breasts against his chest. Her hair coming down around both their faces, gold where the lights get into it and stiff with salt at the ends. He learns her with his mouth: the hinge of her jaw, the hollow at the base of her throat where her pulse is going, the slope of her breast, and she arches into it and says something into his hair that hasn’t got words in it. Her mouth goes to his chest, his collarbone, the side of his neck under his ear. Her hands go down his ribs one at a time, as if she’s counting them for wardrobe.

“Since Monday,” she says against his mouth. “Since the trailer. I stood in the rain with a boy dripping on me for six takes and counted buttons all through them and kept getting forty-one.” She bites his lower lip, not gently. “I’m not counting anything tonight.”

Lying down, her mouth on his is a different thing: slower, heavier, nothing to brace against and nowhere either of them has to be. She kisses him like she’s reading something she means to know by heart, and goes back over the parts she likes. He has wanted this since a window seat in Montecito, and he lets himself know it.

“The male Ohioan,” she says against his ear, low and hushed, in the voice from every nature film ever narrated, “in winter —” her hand goes down his chest to his stomach “— wears a *belt* —” and loses it laughing into his neck, and doesn’t finish.

Her feet are cold, even now. She puts them on his shins on purpose and laughs out loud when he jumps. He gets his hands into her hair and holds her face up where he can see it, with the red and the green of the lights in her eyes, and she lets him look for as long as she can stand it, and then she doesn’t.

At some point he rolls them, and she lets him, for about as long as it takes her to laugh at him for it; then she rolls them back, and the stack of scripts by the bed goes over and slides across the floor in its rubber bands, and they let it. She settles over him with her knees on either side of his hips and both hands spread on his chest, and looks down at him like she’s deciding where to start, and starts everywhere. Her skin tastes of salt, and faintly of oranges.

Reaching up past him to steady herself on the sill she knocks the Christmas lights, and the bulbs are warm against her arm, and one more of them gives out. “Oh, *come on*,” she tells it, and comes back down to him laughing.

Her earring catches in his hair — a small gold hoop — and pins his head to hers, and she stops everything to laugh, holding his head still in both hands while she works it loose. “Hold *still*. I’m stuck in you.” She gets it free, and kisses the place it pulled.

She says his name. Not *Jack*; all of it — *Jack Costigan* — low, in her own voice, looking down at him from a few inches away with the lights behind her head. He stops at the sound of it. She smiles, and puts her mouth back on his.

response: He stops keeping score. He lets the lights and the surf and her weight have all of it, and for a while there isn’t much of him left over apart from the parts she has her hands on.

response: “I want you,” he says into her hair. “I’ve wanted you since the window seat.”
“I know,” Skye says against his throat, very pleased with him. “You’re not subtle, Ohio.”

He catches her wrists and slows her down, and kisses her slower, and she lets him for a while, laughing at him under her breath for it. Then she stops laughing, and slow turns out to be no help to him at all.

s17b.slug: THURSDAY · 11:15 PM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: He wants her. No part of him is pretending otherwise, and she can feel that it isn’t, and he feels her smile about it against his throat.

body.text: He doesn’t want to be good right now. He knows it, and he knows he’s choosing, and he goes on choosing. Her mouth. The lights. Her hips on his through two layers of denim. Her hands going down his stomach to his belt, and he lets them, and the tongue of the buckle comes out of its hole, and it’s a breath, and another breath, before the part of him that’s still awake gets its voice back.
body.else: Under all of it there’s a voice in him, quiet and clear, and it’s his own, and it has known where this was going since the alley. It isn’t loud. It doesn’t have to be. Her hands go down his stomach to his belt, quick and sure, and find the buckle, and there’s no question in them anywhere; she’s smiling against his mouth with the tongue of the buckle halfway out of its hole, and the voice says it.

choices.key: On her bed on Del Playa, with her hands at your belt, you said no. One word.
response: “No.”
Her hands stop. They come off the buckle all at once.
She laughs, one short laugh down at him. “That’s funny,” she says. “That’s a very funny —” She sees his face, and the laugh stops.
For a moment she just stays there above him, with her hair down around her face and her hands open in the air where the buckle was, like somebody who reached for a stair that wasn’t there.
“I didn’t *ask* you anything,” she says, as if that settles it. Then, slower: “I didn’t think I had to. I said not in a *car*.” Half a laugh, with nothing under it. “This isn’t a car.”

She sits back on her heels on the mattress. Her hair has come down on one side. She reaches over the edge of the bed for the man’s flannel on the floor by the rack, and pulls it on, and does up three buttons, the wrong three, and holds it shut at the throat with one fist.
“Oh,” she says. Her mouth has gone into a line he hasn’t seen on her before, straight across, holding something level.
And after a while: “You can go. I’ll drive you. It’s fine.” She starts to get up to look for her keys.
His body hasn’t caught up with what he said. It’s still on the mattress a minute ago, and it lets him know.

He finds his undershirt in the sheets and pulls it on. His shirt he leaves where it landed, and the Carhartt on its hook. He sits down at the foot of the mattress, with his back against the clothes rack, so the hems of her flannels brush his shoulders.
She stops halfway off the bed and looks at him.
“I’m not going anywhere,” he says.
The fist at her throat lets go of the flannel.

Three houses down a party turns its music up, and somebody whoops, and it turns it down again. Skye sits back down. She draws her knees up inside the flannel and looks at him over them, with her arms locked around them and her fingers holding her own wrists hard enough that the knuckles have gone pale.
“Why?” she says.

s18.slug: THURSDAY · 11:40 PM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: Her laptop is open on the floor beside the beach glass, playing something slow and low: a woman’s voice worn soft at the edges, a piano under it, strings coming in behind. “So it isn’t so quiet in here,” Skye said, putting it on, and went back to her end of the bed.

She’s sitting against the wall at the head of the mattress in the flannel, with her knees up and the working half of the lights in her hair. He’s at the foot in his undershirt, his back against the clothes rack. Two mugs of mint tea she went downstairs and made at half past eleven sit on the blanket, going cold in the same place. Whatever was in her face twenty minutes ago, she has put it somewhere. What’s there now is interest, sharp as a new pencil.
She hasn’t said *go* again. She’s been asking him things instead, quick, one after another, the way they run lines at a table read, and she wants every answer.
“What’s a mortal sin.”
“Something serious, that you know is serious, that you do anyway, on purpose. All three.”
“Who decides it’s serious?”
“The Church says what’s serious. Whether you knew, and meant it — that’s between you and God.”
“So it’s the honor system.”
“Pretty much.”
“Does it count if you’re not Catholic?”
“It counts different. What you knew, and what you meant — that’s what counts. That’s in the Catechism, more or less.”
“What does your grandmother think happens to people who do it anyway?”
“She thinks they should go to confession.” He considers his grandmother. “And then eat something.”
“Is it the same rule for boys?”
“Same rule. Same nuns.”
“And did the nuns tell the boys?”
“Every Friday in Lent.”
She takes each answer and keeps it. He can see her keep them, one at a time.
“Is it a sin to want to?”
“No. Wanting’s not the sin. It’s what you do with it. Where you let it live.”
“So you can want me.”
“I can want you.”
“And you do.”
“And I do.”
She’s pleased with that one; he can tell from her eyebrows. “And if you do it anyway? The thing.”
“You go and say so. You mean it. You try not to again.”
“And they let you back in?”
“Every time.”
“That’s a better deal than my industry,” she says. And then, not looking away from him: “When did you decide? Tonight? In the car?”
“A long time before tonight.”
“Before me.”
“Before you.”
“So it isn’t about me.”
“It’s about you too,” Jack says. “It isn’t because of you.”
She turns that over and puts it with the others.
At ten to twelve she puts her tea down on the floor and wraps both arms around her knees.

“Real one,” she says. “Is it God? Does God care where your hands are? Because I’ve met a lot of men who say *God* and mean their mother. I went out with one for a summer. His mother called him during dessert.”
“And don’t tell me you don’t want to. I was *there*.”
She looks at him over her knees. “You threw a game for Him on a road full of cows. I thought it was a reflex.” She waits. “It isn’t, is it.”

“It’s a little bit a debate.”
“Good,” she says. “I win debates.” She wraps both hands around her tea, and looks at him over it like she has all night, which she does.

So he tries. A body says things, he tells her, whether you mean it to or not. She narrows her eyes at that, and points her tea at him to keep going.

“You answered it *second*,” Skye says. “Joke first. I know that move. I *invented* that move.”

And she does. She’s up on her knees on the mattress with an invisible guitar strap over one shoulder and her eyebrows up at her hairline, a youth minister at the end of a lock-in, after the trust falls and before the pizza. “So, guys. Real talk. Your body? Is a *temple*.” She checks the room for agreement. “And you don’t take a temple to the *drive-in*.”
She drops back against the wall. “Fine. Now you.”
So he tries, pamphlet and all, and she lets him. It comes out worse than the youth minister and truer, and somewhere in the middle of it she puts the invisible guitar down.

body: An hour on, the song is long gone and the laptop has wandered off into other songs that she isn’t listening to and he can barely hear. She has had him on the Sixth Commandment, and on the Song of Songs, which she didn’t know was in the Bible and has pulled up on the laptop on her knees and is reading him out of, one finger on the screen. “*Your lips are like a scarlet strand.* This is in the *Bible*. You people have been holding out.” She scrolls. “*Your hair is like a flock of goats*? Jack. That’s a *compliment*?” She has had him on why priests can’t marry, and on whether his grandmother ever kissed anybody but his grandfather, which he has never asked and is never going to. She has had him on Saturdays.
“And what do you *say* in there?”
“The truth.”
“All of it?”
“That’s the whole point.”
“Does the priest ever laugh?”
“One did. He was right to.”

“A body says things,” she says, somewhere in the hour, after he has tried it on her twice. “Fine. Mine’s been saying things on camera since I was a kid. It says whatever’s on the page. It said *I’m saving myself* for three seasons on a lake, with a burrito in my trailer between takes.” She points her tea at him. “So don’t tell me a body can’t lie. It’s the best liar I’ve got.”
“That’s acting,” Jack says. “Everybody knows it’s acting. That’s what acting is.”
“And what’s this?”
“There isn’t a cut.”
She looks at him for that one a good while, and lets him have it, and goes back for more tea.
“Is it hard?” she says. “The not.”
“Yes.”
“How hard?”
“You were there.”
She considers that, and seems to find it fair.
She’s quiet for a minute over her tea. She sets it on the floor and comes forward onto her knees on the mattress, and he can see her bring the big one up from wherever she’s been keeping it.
“Same two people,” she says. “Same bed. Same everything. A man in a robe says some words over us, and then it’s *holy*, and tonight it’s a *sin*?” She leans in. “You’d make love to a notary.”

He laughs, and she doesn’t; she isn’t finished. “I’ve been to nine weddings in this business, Jack. Two of them were for green cards. One was for a network — they told the bride what to wear in a *meeting*. I’ve watched people say the words in front of four hundred people and a string quartet and go home to separate wings of the house. And I’ve seen two people in a makeup trailer at four in the morning, who never signed a thing in their lives, love each other so hard you had to go and wait outside.” She sits back on her heels. “I’ve signed a lot of paper. None of it ever meant I loved anybody. So tell me what the paper does.”

response: “The paper’s the least of it,” Jack says. “The promise is the thing. You don’t say forever with your body before you’ve said it with your life.”
She waits, so he finishes it. “Otherwise your body’s lying. And I’m a bad enough liar with my mouth.”
“And if you say it and then you don’t keep it? People don’t. I’ve been to the weddings.”
“Then you go back and keep it again. That’s most of what keeping is.”
“Who says forever?”
“A Pope. John Paul the Second. Five years of Wednesdays on it.”
“People *went*?”
“Thousands.”
She looks up at the ceiling, considering the thousands. “I’d have gone once,” she says. “For the hats.”

choices.text: “A notary doesn’t stay up with you. That’s the whole difference between a notary and a husband.”
response: “A notary doesn’t stay up with you,” Jack says. “That’s the whole difference between a notary and a husband.” A beat. “Also the stamp.”
She opens her mouth to come back at him and finds she’s laughing instead.

“The paper’s the least of it,” he says, while she’s down. “It’s somebody standing up in front of everybody they know and saying *the rest of it*. With their whole life. And then staying up.” He shrugs. “You don’t say that with your body first. Your body’s not the one that has to keep it.”
She points her tea at him. “The *stamp*,” she says, still going, and he can see her keep the rest of it anyway.

response: “I don’t know if I’ll get it right when it’s my turn,” Jack says. “I just know I want it to be true the first time.”
“*First*,” Skye says.
She sits back against the wall with that, and the knees come up again inside the flannel, and she hasn’t got the next question ready. Eventually she finds one.
“How will you know? When it’s your turn.”
“I won’t, probably. That’s the part I pray about.”
She looks at him like it’s either the dumbest thing she has heard all year or the bravest, and she’s going to need until morning to decide which.

choices.text: “Something happened when I was sixteen. I prayed like somebody was there. Somebody was.”
response: “Something happened when I was sixteen,” Jack says. “I prayed like somebody was there. Somebody was.”
She waits, so he finishes it. “Everything since is me trying to act like I believe that.”
“What’s it like?” she says. “Somebody being there.”
“Like getting caught,” Jack says. “And nobody making you leave.”
She doesn’t push. She asks once. “What happened?”
“Not tonight,” Jack says. And after a while, because she asked it plainly: “My brother took five years. That’s the part I can say.”
“All right,” Skye says, and lets it be, and picks her tea back up.

body: By half past three the laptop is asleep and more of the strand has given up: the dark has come down the left side of the window and across the top, and what’s left of the lights runs down the right side and along the sill. Skye has turned on the mattress to face the wall. She’s sitting with her knees drawn up in the flannel and her back half to him.

She has talked for most of four hours, and for the last quarter of one she hasn’t. He’s at the foot of the bed against the clothes rack, where he sat down at twenty past eleven, with a script she handed him at two o’clock open on his knee — a pilot about a family that runs a motel in Reno, with her notes down the margins in the same downhill capitals — and he hasn’t turned a page since three.

When she does it’s to the wall. “I’ve been looked at for a living since I was eleven,” she says. “Everybody always wanted something. A face. A laugh on the take. A picture for the nephew.” The wall is plaster, with a crack running up it the shape of a river on a map. “And everything I’ve ever done with my body, with anybody, I did like somebody was watching. Like it was for the room.” A pause. “And you’re telling me it was *saying* something. All along.”

“My mother had a word for some of the girls I worked with,” she says. “Not that word. *Reputation*. *That one has a reputation.* She’d write it on the legal pad next to their names, like a height.” Her thumb finds the crack in the plaster. “I was always very careful not to have one where she could see.”

“People look at me and decide,” she says. “It’s the job. They decide, and I let them, and I know what they decided before they do.” She follows the crack up the wall with her thumb as far as she can reach. “Tonight you decided something, and I don’t know what it was. So I’ve been very interested for four hours. I’m good at interested.”
She pulls the cuffs of the flannel down over her hands and holds them shut from the inside. Her eyes go to the window, to the dark half of it.
“Can I ask you something.”
“Yeah.”
“Do you think I’m a slut?”
She goes on, at the window. “Because I like you. And I care what you think, and that doesn’t happen to me.” She stops. “I don’t have a part for this.”
At the foot of the bluff the surf comes in and pulls the gravel back down with it, a long rattle, and comes in again.

Jack doesn’t answer her. He puts the script down on the floor, open, and comes up the mattress on his knees and gets his arms around her from the side — flannel, knees, the cuffs over her hands, all of her he can reach — with his chin by her hair.
The flannel smells of her and of somebody’s cedar closet. Under it her shoulders are all bone and held breath.
She goes stiff. He feels it down the length of her: her back hard against his chest under the flannel, her hands staying where they are inside the cuffs. She doesn’t lean.
“No,” he says, into her hair.
She doesn’t move.
“No. I don’t think anything like that about you. Not once. Not on the beach in November, not in your car, not tonight.”
That would be a good place to stop. She asked him straight, though, so he doesn’t.

“I’ll tell you the other true thing too,” he says. “I don’t like thinking about you with anybody else. Some guy in a trailer. Some guy in a pool house. I hate it, actually. Monday a guy who called me cuz all night stood in the rain with you take after take, and that’s all he did, and I wanted to go and unplug the rain tower.” He hears how that sounds and leaves it. “But that’s mine. That’s me being jealous. It’s about me. What I think about *you* is a different thing.”
She’s still stiff under his arms. He keeps them where they are.
The rest of it is further down, and he has to go and get it.

“The stuff the Church says about this,” he says. “Where your hands go. Who with. I was raised on it, and I was raised to use it on *me*. It’s for judging what I do. That’s what it’s for.” Her hair smells of the Saab and of pencil shavings. “Saturdays I go in with a list. It’s long, and every line on it is mine. I don’t bring anybody else’s. It isn’t my job to.”

“You want to know what’s on it this week? You aren’t. Me in your car is. Me in that trailer. Me tonight, before I said it.” He can feel her listening, all down her back. “My grandmother does it the other way round. She’s got a list for everybody on Glenwood Avenue, and once a month she goes to confession and tells the priest about the weather.”

“You can look at a thing and say it’s wrong. You’re allowed to. You’re supposed to, if somebody asks. But what a person is — you don’t get to decide that. That’s God’s to decide, and He’s a lot more merciful about it than I’d be.” He looked the words up once and kept them. “It’s in the Catechism, near enough. You can say a thing’s grave. The person, you leave to God — to His justice and His mercy. Both of them. It says both.”
He tightens his arms. “So when somebody asks, you tell them the truth about it, straight. You asked me. I did. And then you’re supposed to be hard on yourself and easy on everybody else.”
“I’m very good at the first part.”
It isn’t enough yet. He can feel that it isn’t, all down her back. He goes looking for the rest.

body: At a quarter past four he’s sitting against the wall at the head of the bed and she’s against him, her back to his chest in the flannel, his arms where they were. Past the lights the window hasn’t got anything in it yet. At the foot of the bluff, a long way under the house, the surf comes in slow and goes out slower, and the party three houses down has finally given up and gone to bed.
She’s drawing on his forearm with one fingernail: letters he can’t read, or a map, or nothing.
“What time does the sun come up?” she says. “In December.”
“Ten to seven. Around there.”
“I’ve only ever seen it from a makeup chair.”
“How many candles now?” she says. “On your thing.”
“Two. The third one’s Sunday. That one’s pink.”
“*Pink*?”
“Rose. It’s the rejoicing one.”
“You people have a color for *rejoicing*.” She thinks about that. “What’s the color for this?”
He doesn’t know. Purple, probably. The waiting one.
The fingernail goes on. “Are you going to tell your priest about tonight?”
“Yes.”
“What’ll you say?”
“That I came here. That I wanted to. That I said no.”
“Do you get points for the no?”
“It doesn’t work like points.”
“Everything works like points.” She thinks. “Will he know it’s me?”
“He won’t know your name. And nothing that goes in there comes back out. That’s the deal.”
“Good deal,” she says.
The fingernail stops. “So tell me the rules,” Skye says, into his shirt. “I always want the rules. Is that it? Forever? Till some man in a robe says the words?”
She asks it the way she’d ask a director what the scene is, before she has to go and play it.
He could say forever. It’s the right answer, and it would come out of him sounding like a vow he hasn’t got, and she’d hear that; she hears everything.

He knows what he was like at the turnout, and in the trailer, and here on this mattress at twenty past eleven. He isn’t going to promise her a man he isn’t sure of. And at half past three she asked him if he thought she was a slut, and he wants, more than he wants to be right, to be kind.

“I’m not saying the answer’s always going to be no,” he says. “Not until marriage — I’m not going to tell you that. I don’t know that about me.” Her hair is under his chin. “Just that it’s a big thing for me. And it’s a no right now.”
“I can work with that,” Skye says.
She says it right away, pleased, and he feels her smile against his shirt.

“Cruel’s a strong word,” Skye says. “I’m going to be *thorough*.”
He laughs, and she lies there against him being pleased with the word, and says it once more to herself, trying the weight of it, and keeps it.
“You’re going to be sorry you gave me that one,” she says.
“I know.”

She slides down the mattress and puts her head on his knee in the flannel, and he puts his hand on her hair. Her eyes are shut. She tells him about January with them shut: this room, with the window fixed and the other half of the lights working; the classes she hasn’t picked; a bicycle she’s going to buy and be bad at, in daylight, where everybody can see; a backpack, a real one, with a water bottle in the side. Her voice gets slower around the bicycle and doesn’t quite make it to the end of the backpack.
Nobody stays this late, she says, unless they’re being paid to.

s20.slug: FRIDAY · 5:40 AM · DEL PLAYA, THE PORCH THAT LEANS
body: At twenty to six the sky over the Grove isn’t gray yet, only a black a shade lighter than the rest, with the eucalyptus standing up against it in a ragged row. Cloud is coming in off the water, and up in the southeast, in a gap it hasn’t closed, there’s a lopsided crescent of moon. Somewhere down Del Playa a sprinkler is working at a lawn in the dark and hitting the sidewalk every third pass. A gull goes over. The party three houses down has turned into a porch light and a lawn full of cups.

She walks him out onto the porch in the flannel and his Carhartt, which she took down off the hook over the dress on the way out of her room and put on. It comes to the middle of her thighs, and she has the cuffs turned back twice. The boards lean toward the street. She’s used to the lean; he puts a hand on the post. He’s tired enough that the porch seems to lean more than it does. Her feet are bare on the boards, and she stands one on top of the other to keep half of them warm.

A car goes by slow with its window down and a newspaper comes out of it in a plastic sleeve and lands on the lawn next door, and the car goes on to the next one. A few drops come down on the porch roof and quit.
“The boys come back Sunday,” she says, looking at the empty rack. “They’ll want to know who you were.”
“What’ll you tell them?”
“My cousin from Ohio.”

She looks down Del Playa at the cups on the lawn and the sprinkler and the newspapers in their sleeves, at Las Olas asleep in every direction. “I like it at this hour,” she says. “Everybody’s too asleep to want anything.”
At the top of the steps she takes the Carhartt off and holds it out to him by the collar, and doesn’t let go of it yet. Her face in the porch dark is tired and scrubbed, with all the freckles out.
“You said no,” Skye says. “And you’re still here.”

choices.key: At dawn on the porch that leans she said: you said no, and you’re still here. You said: I’m still here.
response: “I’m still here,” Jack says.
She sits down on the top step in the flannel and holds the Carhartt up by one sleeve while he gets his arm into it, and the other. “Go,” she says, “before I ask you to stay. The sleeping way.”
“Is there a sleeping way?”
“I’ve never tried it.”
She lets go of the sleeve. He goes down the steps, and at the sidewalk he looks back, and she’s still sitting there on the top step with her feet tucked up under the flannel, watching him go.

response: He takes the jacket out of her hand and puts it on and kisses her once, on the top step, quick, while she’s still smiling. “Go on, then,” she says, and gives him a small shove in the chest, and he goes down the steps. At the sidewalk he turns east. She watches him to the corner; he can feel it between his shoulder blades the length of the block.

choices.key: At dawn on the porch that leans she said: you said no, and you’re still here. You asked her to meet you somewhere in daylight.
response: “Meet me somewhere,” he says. “In daylight.”

She laughs at him on the porch at a quarter to six, and the gull on the roof next door answers her. “You’ve *had* daylight. You had me Thursday.” She holds the jacket up and he gets into it. “Sunday,” she says. “Ellery. I’ll teach you to surf. In *December*.” She zips him up to the chin like a mother at a bus stop. “That’s my daylight.”

body: At the corner where Del Playa meets the lane up to campus he takes the RAZR out of the Carhartt and holds the red key down. It wakes into the empty street with its little rising chord, and puts 5:52 on the outer screen, and hunts for a bar, and finds one, and buzzes once in his hand.

body: That’s the only one. Nothing after it, from her or from anybody.
Back down the block a screen door bangs, once, and the street goes quiet again.

He reads it at the corner with the light coming up gray at last behind the eucalyptus. He doesn’t answer it. He puts the phone back in the pocket of the Carhartt, which smells of her room now — mint tea and Sharpie and whatever she puts in her hair — and walks east toward campus between two fences of jasmine gone over for the year. At the edge of the Grove the eucalyptus has got the wet into it already and smells like a medicine cabinet. He goes in under it with his hands in the Carhartt’s pockets and the first of the rain starting, small and cold, on the back of his neck.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom and no surfboards — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that.
